#6064. Why Tech and Crypto Sold Off After the Blue Wave

Why Tech and Crypto Sold Off After the Blue Wave

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • The first market reaction to an election can make a poor foundation for a business plan.
  • It has been revealed that during morning trading on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The first market reaction to an election can make a poor foundation for a business plan. On Nov. 4, stocks and Bitcoin recovered after the Democratic sweep of Congress. By the next U.S. trading morning, that relief rally was coming apart.

It has been revealed that during morning trading on Nov. 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 4%. Bitcoin also reversed course: Bitcoin.com reported a Bitstamp low of $75,468 by 10:55 a.m. Eastern, after the cryptocurrency had traded above $81,000 the previous day.

According to recent reports, the reversal makes a simple political explanation difficult. The election result had not changed. Investors were reassessing what it might mean for businesses and assets whose valuations depended on continued growth, access to financing and confidence in the future.

For entrepreneurs, the useful question is how much of a business strategy still works when those assumptions become less generous.

The blue wave introduced another uncertainty for the AI buildout. Reuters reported concern that Democratic victories could bring closer scrutiny of data-center expansion. Chipmakers, data-center operators and companies supplying that expansion came under pressure as investors considered the possibility of slower development.

According to recent reports, these were concerns about possible future restrictions. Markets can mark down a manufacturer because a project might face delays, long before an agency or legislature acts. Expectations can change a valuation before a rule changes an operating plan.

For a developer, even a temporary delay can change the economics. Equipment has to be financed, contracts carry obligations and interest can accumulate before customers start paying. A project can remain technologically promising while becoming less attractive at its original cost and timetable.

In a recent development, those concerns were already building before election night. A separate Reuters report described investors questioning returns on enormous AI investments and the use of debt to fund them. The political shift added another uncertainty to that existing debate; it did not create every weakness in the trade.

Industry observers note that company results mattered, too. In its November 4 earnings release, Qualcomm reported quarterly handset revenue of $5.137 billion, down 26% from a year earlier. It also warned of rising semiconductor input costs. These were operating pressures with their own implications for earnings, irrespective of which party won Congress.

In a recent development, for a founder selling an ambitious growth story, that is the uncomfortable part. Investors may still believe in the technology while demanding stronger evidence that expansion will produce an acceptable return.

It has been revealed that bitcoin’s decentralized design does not make its price independent of financial markets. Its network operates without a central owner, but people still buy and sell it with finite capital, changing risk preferences and sometimes borrowed money.

When investors become more defensive, assets with very different underlying purposes can fall together. A trader reducing exposure does not need to abandon a long-term belief in Bitcoin to sell it. The immediate priority may simply be to reduce losses or free up cash.

Leverage can make that process faster. Coinbase International Exchange’s trading rules, for example, provide for automatic liquidation when account equity falls below maintenance requirements. Closing leveraged positions can add further pressure to an existing move. The mechanism helps explain how selling can accelerate without a new piece of political news arriving each time prices fall.

According to recent reports, there was evidence of forced closures across crypto. Bitcoin.com cited Coinglass figures showing roughly $839 million in liquidations over the preceding 24 hours, including approximately $741 million in bullish positions. That window spans two trading days, and the figures measure positions liquidated rather than an equivalent amount of cash withdrawn.

The simultaneous sell-off is consistent with investors cutting risk, with leverage amplifying the pressure. It does not establish that the same investors sold both markets, or that the blue wave alone caused Bitcoin’s decline.

The most useful response to this kind of volatility is a closer look at the operating plan. A changing market can reveal dependencies that were easy to overlook when financing was available and valuations were rising.

Industry observers note that start with funding. If the next equity round takes six months longer, which commitments still have to be paid? If a loan becomes more expensive or a project approval takes longer, does the business have enough cash to reach its next meaningful milestone?

Then examine demand. An AI company should be able to show what customers pay for, how often they return and whether delivering the service produces a sustainable margin. A crypto business should understand how lower asset prices, thinner liquidity or increased withdrawals would affect its operations.

Political assumptions deserve the same treatment. An expected approval, friendly administration or proposed law may improve the outlook. Put those benefits in a scenario that can be tested, and identify how the business operates if they arrive later than expected.

This exercise can produce specific decisions: stage a capital project, negotiate more flexible supplier terms or prioritize a product customers already pay to use. It is more useful than trying to predict the next market rebound.

Recent findings suggest that the post-midterm reversal does not settle the long-term case for AI or digital assets. It does show how rapidly market enthusiasm can disappear while a tech giant’s spending obligations remain.

It has been revealed that the blue wave was part of the context. Earnings, financing costs, expectations for infrastructure growth and leveraged trading also shaped the environment. Assigning the entire move to one election result would leave founders with an incomplete explanation.

A company cannot control the next election or the next wave of selling. It can control how much of its future depends on a favorable outcome. That is where the work should begin.

In a recent development, the first market reaction to an election can make a poor foundation for a business initiative. On Nov. 4, stocks and Bitcoin recovered after the Democratic sweep of Congress. By the next U.S. trading morning, that relief rally was coming apart.

In a recent development, during morning trading on Nov. 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 4%. Bitcoin also reversed course: Bitcoin.com reported a Bitstamp low of $75,468 by 10:55 a.m. Eastern, after the cryptocurrency had traded above $81,000 the previous day.

It has been revealed that the reversal makes a simple political explanation difficult. The election result had not changed. Investors were reassessing what it might mean for businesses and assets whose valuations depended on continued growth, access to financing and confidence in the future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The following story contains spoilers for VisionQuest.

LIKE WandaVision AND Agatha All Along before it, VisionQuest turned out to be among the best Marvel projects to be released in the post-Endgame era. And given that the series was billed as the conclusion to the trilogy that those prior two shows set up, that should come as no surprise. While many Marvel Cinematic Universe movies and shows in the last five years have struggled to figure out what works and what doesn’t—and what manages to resonate with audiences over time—these shows, released over the course of a nearly six-year span, have clearly understood that the recipe for success is pretty simple: a slightly raised concept, and some characters people really love.

Recent findings suggest that visionQuest took a formula that felt like something of a hybrid of what made the other two reveals successful and rode it. Where WandaVision had a super high concept (Wanda turning her world into a surreal series of sitcom references), returning stars (both Elizabeth Olsen and Paul Bettany led the show), and latest characters people became obsessed with (Kathryn Hahn’s Agatha), Agatha All Along then introduced the idea of bringing in a vital new character in Wanda and Vision’s son Billy (Joe Locke) to go along with the returning Agatha.

In a recent development, visionQuest splits the atom by pairing Bettany with a returning James Spader as Ultron (truly fantastic throughout) and introducing Ruaridh Mollica as Tommy, Wanda and Vision’s other superpowered son. The show’s consistently strong, surprising, and well-paced writing from showrunner Terry Matalas—to go along with fun latest characters like the Paladin (Todd Stashwick) and E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire)—made it an easy, fun, watchable hit. And it helped that in the end, it came with a punch.

The show continued to expand on Vision becoming human, something Bettany has proven to be brilliant at during the course of his time in the MCU, but it also gave layers to Spader’s Ultron, proving that the franchise can allow some of its iconic villains to stick around and play in shades of moral gray.

By the end of the show, Vision, Tommy, and Billy have made it through the adventure, discovered themselves, and reunited as the family unit we’ve long known they were meant to be. There was just one lingering question: Where’s mom?

Sources indicate that visionQuest asks the question near the end. Elizabeth Olsen’s Wanda Maximoff was the most popular character (and briefly became one of the best villains) in the MCU in the aftermath of Avengers: Endgame; WandaVision was a massive smash, hitting during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and becoming the closest thing to water cooler talk material that anyone could get at the time. Olsen’s performance, nominated for an Emmy, was one of the most important reasons why.

She took a more sinister arc in the following year’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, and—spoiler alert—appeared to be “dead” at the end of the movie. Which puts a serious wrinkle into the possibility of her reuniting with her robotic husband and immaculately conceived sons.

According to recent reports, but this is the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and we’re talking about stories based off of comic books. There’s always a way.

Sources indicate that of course she is! Wanda Maximoff is one of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s most beloved characters, and Elizabeth Olsen’s performance as her is truly fantastic. You didn’t think Kevin Feige would leave her alone beneath a mountain, did you?

Sure, it’s been more than four years since we last saw the Scarlet Witch at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, but as the credits scene for VisionQuest (likely a moment taken right out of next month’s Avengers: Doomsday) reveals us: She’s back. Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) picks up the bit of mountain she was crushed underneath, and her eyes rocket open in a Jon Snow–esque awakening. “Scarlet Witch, awaken,” Doom says. “Your power will be mine.”.

It’s not hard to read into what’s going on here. It’s clear that in Doomsday, Doom is recruiting from some of our existing and most powerful Marvel heroes in an attempt to fuel his own takeover of the world. In the 2015 Secret Wars comic, Doom saves the universe from destruction after incursions (the collision of parallel universes) threaten to destroy everything; the result finds unexpected allyships as Doom takes his place as God Emperor. In that story, Doom’s second-in-command is Doctor Strange… someone we’ve already seen have quite the experience with Wanda (in Multiverse of Madness). Will they wind up allied once again in Doomsday?

It has been revealed that the news of Wanda’s return also comes as we learn that her on-screen hubby will also be in Doomsday. “I got to hang out with Paul Bettany, who I love,” Anthony Mackie mentioned in a recent interview, spilling some of the beans.

If VisionQuest was the conclusion of the WandaVision trilogy—and a darn good one—it sounds like Doomsday could feature a full-on Wanda and Vision reunion. And what Marvel fan who’s been along for this ride (and stuck it through to this point) wouldn’t be excited for that? Let’s get the family back together, shall we?

#6062. 10 Grammy 2027 nomination snubs and surprises, from Harry Styles to Björk

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3044 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

10 Grammy 2027 nomination snubs and surprises, from Harry Styles to Björk

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that harry Styles got 0 nominations and Raye tied a record with 11.
  • Industry observers note that anyone who opened the 2027 Grammy nominations expecting to see the year's biggest sellers at the top found a different set of names.
  • In a recent development, the Academy describes its ballot as open to everyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that harry Styles got 0 nominations and Raye tied a record with 11. See 10 acts the 2027 Grammy nominations snubbed or surprised.

Industry observers note that anyone who opened the 2027 Grammy nominations expecting to see the year's biggest sellers at the top found a different set of names. Voters at the Recording Academy reshuffled who counts this year, and several acts with the most commercial weight came away with little or nothing to show for their year. Rapper A$AP Rocky received no nominations at all, according to Rolling Stone. His shutout was not an isolated case among artists with large followings. Artists with a strong year with listeners had no assurance of a place on this ballot.

In a recent development, the Academy describes its ballot as open to everyone. Harvey Mason jr., the Recording Academy's CEO, told The Associated Press that "it’s inspiring to see musicians at every stage of their careers represented." Career stage predicted little this year, though, because veterans and first-time nominees landed on both sides of the line. The two sides do not stand on equal footing. An act left off the ballot has no further chance this cycle, while every surprise nominee still has to win over voters again in final voting, which runs from Dec. 10 to Jan. 7. The Academy will name the winners at the 69th Grammy Awards on Feb. 7 in Los Angeles, according to St. Louis Public Radio. That timing is why the upsets matter now, since they show what voters valued before anyone has handed out a trophy.

Recent findings suggest that W Magazine set out to find the biggest upsets of the 2027 Grammy nominations. The first surprise sits at the very top of the ballot, where for the first time all six of the most-nominated artists are women. Several men who had substantial years, Harry Styles among them, drew less recognition than expected. The upsets also reach well past chart stars. Madonna and the women of country music appear among them, and so does a masked experimental duo that few casual listeners know, which earned multiple nominations in the Best New Artist race. The duo comes from Quebec, according to CBC Music, and it now competes on the same ballot as a pop icon. The acts that follow include both artists left off the ballot and artists who forced their way onto it, and each kind helps explain the other. Together they show the Academy rewarding something other than the year's biggest names, and the slides that follow show where that line fell.

Harry Styles went from the Grammys' top prize to no nominations at all. Rolling Stone reports that his album Harry's House won Album of the Year in 2023, and that Styles was left off the 2027 ballot entirely, with zero nominations. That result is not a near miss in the all-genre races at the top. The shutout covers every category on the ballot, including the genre awards.

Styles did not make his fresh record with a new team. He worked again with Kid Harpoon and Tyler Johnson on Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally, according to Rolling Stone, so the album reunited him with collaborators from his past work. That reunion did not bring the nominations his last album had earned.

Styles also came into this cycle with well-known hits behind him. His earlier songs include "As It Was" and "Watermelon Sugar," according to W Magazine, and listeners still connect him with both. Those hits gave him a large audience going into this year. Neither that audience nor his return to familiar collaborators earned the upcoming album a place in a single race. His case shows that an artist's past record carried little weight on this year's ballot, even for a singer who had won the biggest award only a few years earlier.

Three years after Album of the Year, Styles has no nomination to show for his newly introduced record.

Raye's upset is an outsider leading the Grammy ballot, not a favorite being passed over. She topped every artist with 11 nominations, according to W Magazine. That total matches the most any woman has earned in a single year, a record Beyoncé set and Raye ties rather than breaks. She reached it with little history at the Grammys. Before this year she had four career nominations and had never won, according to The Associated Press. Voters had nominated her before, but never on anything close to this scale, and now they place her at the head of the field. She arrives at the top of the ballot as a newcomer, not as an established star adding one more honor.

Raye competes in the races that judge every genre at once. The Associated Press reports that her song "Where Is My Husband!" is up for record of the year and that she, Rosalía, Taylor Swift and Olivia Rodrigo are among the album of the year nominees. Rosalía is next in the nomination count with nine. Her closest rival is also her opponent in the biggest category, so Raye's lead gives her no margin where it matters most.

Rosalía also arrives with a top prize that Raye has never won. Her album "Lux" won album of the year at the Latin Grammys, according to The Associated Press. Raye's nomination count reveals how many races she entered, not what she will win. The ballot has made her the year's breakthrough, and whether that breakthrough becomes her first Grammy is still open.

According to recent reports, madonna is back on the Grammy ballot, but voters stopped short of placing her among the year's frontrunners. She earned four nominations for the 2027 awards with her fresh album, Confessions on a Dance Floor: Part 2, according to W Magazine. E! News reports that the Recording Academy had gone 16 years without nominating her before this year. Her return to the ballot is a real comeback after a long absence. None of the four came in the Big Four, the all-genre categories at the top of the ballot. Voters welcomed her back but kept her out of the races that decide the night.

The nominations reward newly introduced music that listeners had already embraced, not a long career. Fans streamed the album 13.07 million times on Spotify $SPOT on its first full day, according to chartdata figures reported by CBC. The album also drew praise as personal work rather than a return to old hits. "This is Madonna as a memoirist. This is Madonna as a storyteller," music journalist Emilie Hanskamp noted. A large audience and serious praise still did not carry her into the top races.

In a recent development, voters' respect for Madonna's work has never been in doubt, and the new nods bring her career total to 32 Grammy nominations. They gave her a place on the ballot this year, but they did not give her a chance at the night's biggest prizes. Her legacy was already secure. The open question was whether voters still see her as a frontrunner.

This year, their answer is not yet.

This year's ballot leaned toward women, but that lean stopped short of the young women behind some of the year's biggest pop runs. Gracie Abrams, Stella Lefty and Sienna Spiro each came off a strong year, but only Spiro drew a nomination, in Best Upcoming Artist, while Abrams and Lefty were left off the ballot entirely, according to W Magazine. Where the Recording Academy recognized these three at all, it treated them as newcomers rather than as artists ready for the top races.

Abrams aimed highest and was turned away both in the all-genre field and in her own genre. She submitted her album for Album of the Year and Best Pop Vocal Album, E! News reports, and her single "Hit the Wall" went unrecognized along with the album. Before this year, voters had recognized her as a newcomer and as a duet partner. Her first nomination came in 2024 in Best Latest Artist, the same category that holds Spiro's only nomination this year. In 2025 voters nominated her for Best Pop Duo Performance for "Us," a track she shared with Taylor Swift. This year she asked voters to judge her on her own in the biggest fields, and they declined.

Sources indicate that lefty had a hit and still drew no nominations. E! News reports that "Boston" was a hit for her, yet voters named her in no category, from the newcomer race to the top fields. A hit song did not guarantee a nomination this year.

Recent findings suggest that spiro's nomination confirmed a verdict another awards show had already reached. She won Best Newly introduced Artist at this year's VMAs, and Grammy voters likewise recognized her as a new artist. Her one nomination is in Best New Artist, not for her song "Die on This Hill." Grammy voters agreed with the VMAs that Spiro is a new artist to watch, and they went no further than that.

Audrey Hobert and her brother, Malcolm Todd, were both shut out of the 2027 Grammy nominations, according to W Magazine. The miss was total for two sibling pop acts whom many expected to see in the Best Latest Artist race. That expectation came from buzz, not from a forecast. Unnamed observers had speculated about Best New Artist bids for both, and neither the Recording Academy nor any named source had made that call. Their shutout is a test of whether talk of a breakout turns into a place on the ballot, and for this pair it did not.

Hobert had the stronger claim to a breakout. Rolling Stone reports that she had a Billboard Hot 100 entry with her song "Sue Me." With that chart entry, she had evidence behind the Best Newly introduced Artist talk around her, not just rumor. Voters still left her out of the new-artist field. No reason for the omission has surfaced, so her miss is a verdict without an explanation.

Todd's music reached the ballot even though he did not. Rolling Stone reports that Don Toliver sampled Todd's "Chest Pain (I Love)" on "E85," and voters nominated that track for Best Rap Song and Best Melodic Rap Performance. Those nominations belong to Toliver's record, and Todd does not count as a nominee on it. Both races are in rap categories, far from the new-artist race where the speculation had placed Todd. A sample on another artist's hit gave him no credit of his own with voters.

It has been revealed that the sibling Best New Artist story needed both of them to get in. Instead, voters passed over each of them, and neither breakout earned a nomination.

In a recent development, women made this year's surprise in country by taking a whole Grammy race outright. No man is in the running for Best Contemporary Country Album, because for the first time all five nominees are women, according to W Magazine. Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith, Ella Langley, Megan Moroney and Kacey Musgraves fill the slate, CBC News reports, and that makes the result a breakthrough rather than a grievance. In this race the story is how completely women held the field, not who was left off it.

Industry observers note that langley is at the center of the sweep with seven nominations, according to CBC News. Only Raye and Rosalía have more, and Langley's total ties her with Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and Miranda Lambert. Lambert reached that group partly through Langley's hit, "Choosin' Texas." She co-wrote the song and shares four of Langley's nominations. Two country women now stand among the year's most-nominated artists, and part of each woman's total comes from the same song.

The women swept only half of country's album field. CBC News reports that country albums now compete in separate contemporary and traditional categories, and the sweep took place in the contemporary one. None of the five women from that race appears among the traditional nominees, so their hold belongs to one style of country. Langley and Musgraves do reach past the album race, with nominations for Best Country Solo Performance as well.

The country women's breakthrough is real, but it is a takeover of contemporary country, and whether it extends to the rest of the genre is still open.

Recent findings suggest that voters gave Noah Kahan far less recognition than his audience would suggest. The singer has been hugely popular since 2022, but his only nomination this year is for a folk album, according to W Magazine. This year, voters measured him against folk records rather than against the year's biggest names.

Sources indicate that kahan missed the top of the ballot, where artists from every genre compete. None of his work appeared in the races for record, song or album of the year, according to Quartz. Several unnamed experts had expected him to land in those races, according to Hollywood Reporter forecasts reported by Quartz. A nomination in any of the three would have put him in contention against the whole field rather than against folk records alone. The distance between those predictions and his single nomination makes his result an upset rather than a routine genre outcome.

Industry observers note that voters were judging a different album from the one that made Kahan famous. He broke out with Stick Season in 2022, according to W Magazine, while the album on this year's ballot is The Great Divide. The result passes no verdict on the songs that built his following and applies to the latest album alone. Kahan kept his public response short. "Life goes on," he wrote in a tweet on nominations Monday.

He can still win the folk race. This year he did not earn a place among the contenders in the all-genre races.

This year's left-field pop acts reached the Grammy ballot through dance and electronic music. Voters named Slayyyter, Tinashe and Underscores as rivals in a single race, Best Dance/Electronic Recording, according to W Magazine. Three acts from outside the mainstream now compete in one category. Slayyyter and Tinashe also face each other for Best Dance Pop Recording. Underscores is absent from that second race, so the three acts did not share equally in the recognition. Slayyyter earned four nominations in all, according to St. Louis Public Radio, and she is a real presence in the genre's categories this year.

Sources indicate that slayyyter was no unknown by the time voters filled out their ballots. She gave a breakthrough performance at Lollapalooza. She also played to much larger audiences over the year. In the spring she took the stage at Coachella, and she appeared on national television for the first time as a guest on "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon," according to St. Louis Public Radio. She had performed for major festival crowds and a television audience across the country well before the nominations came out. Her nominations went to an artist whom many listeners had already seen for themselves.

Listeners who have not yet heard Slayyyter, Tinashe or Underscores can start with this year's dance categories.

Industry observers note that justin Bieber did not lose a close race this year. He is missing from the ballot entirely. His album Swag earned a Grammy nomination, according to CBC Music, so voters had backed his previous album. Yet Swag II, the album that followed it, brought him not a single nod for the 2027 awards, according to W Magazine. Bieber also submitted the songs "Everything Hallelujah" and "Speed Demon," and neither one made the cut. Voters turned down his whole year, not a single release. For an artist the Academy had nominated so recently, that is a clean break rather than a quiet miss.

It has been revealed that voters stopped rewarding Bieber before they stopped nominating him. He holds two Grammy wins over his career, yet CBC Music reports that he left the 2026 ceremony without a trophy. His most recent turn with the Academy ended in a nomination and no win. Seen across two years, his standing with voters fell from a loss on Grammy night to no place on the ballot at all.

It has been revealed that the Academy had not pushed him aside on that earlier night, though. Bieber performed at the 68th Grammys on Feb. 1, his first time on the Grammy stage in four years, according to CBC Music, and he went home empty-handed the same evening. Organizers wanted him on the show even as voters passed him over for awards.

On this evidence, his zero reflects what this year's voters prized rather than a break between Bieber and the Grammys as a whole. They moved past an artist they had nominated not long ago.

Recent findings suggest that grammy voters recognized Angine de Poitrine on two fronts at once, as a newcomer and in the rock field. Voters placed the experimental rock duo in the Best New Artist race, according to Rolling Stone, so it now faces every other act hoping to break through this year. That newcomer race was not its only nomination. Its four nominations in all, CBC Music reports, reach well past Best New Artist into Best Rock Performance, Best Rock Album and Best Alternative Music Performance. Three of the four fall in rock and alternative categories, so the duo's place on the ballot rests on more than a single nomination as a new name. Angine de Poitrine is still only a contender, though, and it has won nothing yet.

For Canadian listeners, these nominations confirm a rise they had already watched. The Canadian duo won both the Polaris Music Prize and the Song Prize in September, according to CBC Music, and it reached the Grammy ballot with those honors already in hand. The duo had also announced a 2027 tour before the nominations came out. Fans were already waiting for those reveals, however Grammy voters decided. Much of the Grammy audience is now hearing the name for the first time, while listeners in Canada heard the music months ago.

Recent findings suggest that with this pick, voters did not overrule the year's buzz. They caught up with buzz that had already built in Canada.

#6060. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1154 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.
  • The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy.
  • A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Industry observers note that sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

Sources indicate that the window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

According to recent reports, competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”.

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each latest model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

Industry observers note that the data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

According to recent reports, learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

In a recent development, jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its major commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”.

In a recent development, finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”.

According to recent reports, prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”.

In a recent development, swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction organization I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

Industry observers note that A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments manufacturer whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, stated it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”.

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

Industry observers note that to repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one states, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

Sources indicate that in AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

5 Businesses I Wouldn’t Start in 2027 — and 5 Models I’d Look at Instead

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Recent findings suggest that search “best businesses to start” and you’ll see the same ideas on repeat: dropshipping, influencing, a generic marketing agency, something on Amazon.
  • After nearly a decade in ecommerce and online business, I’ve learned that the business model matters almost as much as the entrepreneur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that search “best businesses to start” and you’ll see the same ideas on repeat: dropshipping, influencing, a generic marketing agency, something on Amazon. Technically, they can all still work. But “can work” and “where I’d put my time and money today” are two very different things.

After nearly a decade in ecommerce and online business, I’ve learned that the business model matters almost as much as the entrepreneur. A great operator can fight through a difficult model, but why choose one that demands enormous time, has razor-thin margins or depends on constantly finding your next customer?

In a recent development, heading into 2027, I’m drawn to three things: leverage, recurring revenue and systems. Here are five businesses I’d think twice about starting from scratch, and what I’d consider instead.

A few years ago, the playbook was simple: land a few local clients at $1,000 or $2,000 a month, outsource the work and scale. But everyone got the memo. Generalist agencies now compete with freelancers, offshore teams, in-house hires and increasingly capable AI tools.

Sources indicate that solve one expensive problem for one type of business. Help dental practices follow up with leads who never scheduled. Build AI customer-service workflows for ecommerce brands. Automate reminders and customer reactivation for home-service companies.

Recent findings suggest that the opportunity isn’t selling AI; businesses can access that themselves. It’s knowing what to automate and connecting it to a real outcome. “Social media management” is a vague line item, while recovering thousands of dollars in lost leads is easy to understand. Sell the outcome, not the technology.

The idea that you can open a Seller Central account, list a few products after work and enjoy effortless income is increasingly disconnected from reality. Sourcing, pricing, Buy Box competition, inventory, customer service and account health all demand attention. For someone who wants to become an operator, that’s fine. But many professionals want ecommerce exposure without creating a second full-time job.

For people with more capital than time, a professionally managed ecommerce storefront may be worth a look. The owner funds and owns the store, while an experienced team handles day-to-day operations for a fee or a share of profits, much like a property owner hiring a property manager. These investors aren’t looking for something else to do. They’re looking for something else to own.

Recent findings suggest that it isn’t risk-free. Marketplaces shift, sales fluctuate and projected income is never guaranteed income, so vet who actually operates the store and how profits are calculated before you commit.

It has been revealed that the pitch is irresistible: no inventory, your supplier ships the order and you pocket the difference. But acquiring the customer is the hard part. A store selling products that hundreds of other websites also sell has little competitive advantage, and you’re often dependent on paid advertising and on finding products before competitors pile in.

It has been revealed that think beauty, pet products, specialty foods, personal care or hobby consumables. The category matters less than the economics. Ask yourself: If I spend $40 acquiring this customer today, can they be worth $200 to me over the next two years?

According to recent reports, an ad stops producing the moment you turn it off. A loyal customer base, an email list and a recognizable brand can become more valuable every year.

Expertise used to be nearly enough: record six hours of video, build a landing page, charge $997. Today, information is abundant, including through AI, and people are reluctant to pay premium prices for it. Information isn’t scarce anymore; real results are.

Sources indicate that build several specific products that solve narrow problems, such as a template, calculator, workflow, database, paid community or small software tool, and create content for the audience they serve. Someone who knows Airbnb could skip the “$997 Masterclass” and offer a profitability calculator, a cleaning-checklist system, guest-message templates and a paid newsletter on market changes. That ecosystem is much harder to replace with a single AI prompt.

Personal brands are powerful, but they can become cages. If revenue disappears when you stop posting or showing your face online, you’ve created income, not necessarily an independent business. You might love posting three videos a day at 25. Will you still want to at 35?

According to recent reports, this is the filter I’d apply to almost any opportunity: Can this eventually work without me? It doesn’t need to be hands-off on day one, but there should be a path from founder-dependent to system-dependent. Can someone else handle customer service? Can sales become repeatable? Can procedures be documented? Can customers keep buying while you’re on vacation?

If every key function leads back to you, that’s not freedom. It’s self-employment with a nicer title.

It has been revealed that the business I’m watching in 2027 isn’t really an idea. It’s leverage. AI gives one employee leverage. Software gives a small company leverage. Recurring revenue gives customer acquisition leverage. A management team gives an owner leverage. Capital gives an investor leverage. And systems give entrepreneurs perhaps the most valuable form of all: time.

According to recent reports, so instead of asking, “What’s the hottest business to start?” ask: What can I build or own today that becomes less dependent on my time as it grows? If you have little capital but plenty of time, an AI automation service may fit. If you understand products and branding, consider a niche consumer brand. If you have expertise but don’t want to become an influencer, digital products can turn it into an asset. And if you have capital but little spare time, a professionally managed business may deserve a closer look.

In a recent development, the best business isn’t always the one that makes the most money today. It may be the one that eventually stops needing you to make every dollar. After all, your time is precious.

Sources indicate that search “best businesses to start” and you’ll see the same ideas on repeat: dropshipping, influencing, a generic marketing agency, something on Amazon. Technically, they can all still work. But “can work” and “where I’d put my time and money today” are two very different things.

After nearly a decade in ecommerce and online business, I’ve learned that the business model matters almost as much as the entrepreneur. A great operator can fight through a difficult model, but why choose one that demands enormous time, has razor-thin margins or depends on constantly finding your next customer?

Recent findings suggest that heading into 2027, I’m drawn to three things: leverage, recurring revenue and systems. Here are five businesses I’d think twice about starting from scratch, and what I’d consider instead.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple's US dollar-backed stablecoin RLUSD has set a upcoming record by surpassing PayPal USD (PYUSD) in market capitalization to cement its position as a top stablecoin globally.

Recent data from CoinGecko demonstrates that RLUSD's market cap has grown to around $2.71 billion, enabling it to surpass its competitor, PayPal's stablecoin, with a market cap of around $2.69 billion.

This milestone was achieved less than two years after Ripple's formal introduction of RLUSD in December 2024, underscoring its rapid growth in the crypto market.

A prominent XRP Ledger validator, Vet, also commented on this development to underscore the increasing significance of RLUSD in the stablecoin industry.

"RLUSD is now a Top 5 USD backed stablecoin. On its way to be in Top 3," Vet commented.

Vet noted Ripple's long-standing contribution to building the XRP Ledger. He added that the increasing adoption of RLUSD could potentially lead to faster adoption of the blockchain by traditional financial institutions.

Vet stressed the increasing relevance of RLUSD's rising payment volume and increased use of the stablecoin on the XRP Ledger.

He also noted that RLUSD has opened the door to numerous integrations with banks and crypto exchanges.

The XRP Ledger validator further noted that these integrations could motivate financial institutions to not only run infrastructure to support the XRPL but also integrate other tokenized assets on it.

This new record for RLUSD comes on the back of several key institutional partnerships and exchange integrations for RLUSD that Ripple has been announcing recently.

On Oct. 28, Ripple announced a partnership with Coinbase to provide RLUSD for retail and institutional customers across Coinbase Exchange, Coinbase Prime and its retail trading app.

As part of the partnership, Coinbase also announced support for RLUSD across different blockchain networks such as the XRP Ledger, Ethereum and Base.

On the other hand, Ripple's partnership with banking giant BNY, which is the custodian of reserves for RLUSD, is also deepening.

Besides this, Ripple has also managed to secure support from Standard Chartered, which debuted institutional custody services for RLUSD on the XRP Ledger back in October.

Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a newly introduced setback for its Starlink rival

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 15, 2026 at 2:16 pm.
  • A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket malfunctioned about 10 minutes after liftoff Sunday and failed to reach orbit, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle tech giant’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.
  • It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 15, 2026 at 2:16 pm.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket malfunctioned about 10 minutes after liftoff Sunday and failed to reach orbit, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle tech giant’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA noted it doesn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it will work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as promptly as possible.

Amazon Leo stated in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term aims for Vulcan.”.

In a recent development, the rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

The anomaly came about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn, according to Spaceflight Now. The Centaur is powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris.

Industry observers note that spaceflight Now also reported that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t identified the cause.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had debuted 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Recent findings suggest that melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

Sources indicate that in June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it looks an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

In a recent development, ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the Newly introduced Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#6054. 4 artists who boycotted the Grammys and what they were protesting

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1859 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

4 artists who boycotted the Grammys and what they were protesting

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four artists who boycotted the Grammys, from the 1989 rap category dispute to The Weeknd's 2021 protest, and what each one mentioned about the awards.
  • According to recent reports, A Grammy is the most visible form of peer recognition the music business offers.
  • Sources indicate that artists who boycotted the Grammys have aimed at different targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four artists who boycotted the Grammys, from the 1989 rap category dispute to The Weeknd's 2021 protest, and what each one mentioned about the awards.

According to recent reports, A Grammy is the most visible form of peer recognition the music business offers. Declining to take part in the awards is a statement in itself. The Recording Academy's members vote on the honors. An artist who steps away from that system is making a public point about how it works.

Sources indicate that artists who boycotted the Grammys have aimed at different targets. Some objected to how a genre was handled on the broadcast. Others objected to how nominees are picked in the first place. In each case, the protest put a specific complaint on the record.

This article looks at four of those protests. It is a selection, not a ranking and not a complete history. Other musicians have also criticized the awards or pulled their work over the years, and they are not covered here.

The four cases stretch across more than three decades. In 1989, DJ Jazzy Jeff & the Fresh Prince stayed away after the Recording Academy chose not to televise the first rap award. In 1991, Sinéad O'Connor declined to take part in the ceremony and turned down the award she won. Frank Ocean kept his 2016 album Blonde out of contention for the 2017 awards by not submitting it. In 2021, The Weeknd mentioned he would stop letting his label submit his music.

It has been revealed that taken together, the cases show how the grievances shifted. The earliest dispute was about whether a genre belonged on the main broadcast. O'Connor's 1991 objection was broader, aimed at the commercialism of the awards. The two most recent were about process. They asked who decides what gets nominated and whether the institution reflects the artists it rewards.

The word boycott also covers more than one tactic. An artist can refuse to attend. An artist can refuse an award after winning it. An artist can also withhold music from the submission process entirely. That last option carries a real cost. A record that is never entered cannot win anything.

Industry observers note that the Recording Academy has since changed part of its nomination process. In April 2021, it declared that it was ending the anonymous nomination review committees, the panels The Weeknd had criticized. Nominations in the affected categories were to be decided by the Academy's voting members instead.

The slides that follow explain who protested, what each artist objected to and what came after.

Recent findings suggest that DJ Jazzy Jeff & the Fresh Prince boycotted the 1989 Grammys because the Recording Academy chose not to present the first Best Rap Performance award on the televised broadcast. The duo won that award anyway, for "Parents Just Don't Understand.".

In a recent development, the pair was DJ Jazzy Jeff, born Jeffrey Townes, and rapper Will Smith. Both came from Philadelphia. Their winning track came from He's the DJ, I'm the Rapper, released in 1988.

In a recent development, the song is a comic story about a teenager at odds with his parents. In the first verse, his mother takes him back-to-school shopping and picks out clothes he can't stand. Its broad, family-friendly humor gave the record a mainstream audience.

That audience was part of the dispute. A rap song heard well beyond rap's core fans was being honored off camera.

Industry observers note that other rap acts joined the duo in staying away from the ceremony. Their objection was narrow. They did not reject the Grammys as an institution. They rejected the decision to keep the new rap category off the main show.

By 1989, rap was not a fresh arrival on the charts. The Sugarhill Gang's "Rapper's Delight," released in 1979, became a U.S. Top 40 hit. That was roughly a decade before the Academy created a rap category.

In a recent development, the same ceremony introduced another genre award that drew a separate dispute. Jethro Tull won the first Grammy for Best Hard Rock/Metal Performance Vocal or Instrumental, beating Metallica. That result had nothing to do with the rap boycott. Both episodes involved genres the Academy was only starting to recognize with categories of their own.

According to recent reports, the duo's relationship with the awards continued after the boycott. DJ Jazzy Jeff & the Fresh Prince won a second Grammy for "Summertime" at the 1992 ceremony.

It has been revealed that smith's career also widened promptly. The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air premiered on NBC in 1990, with Smith in the lead role. As a solo artist, he later won Grammys for "Men in Black" and "Gettin' Jiggy wit It.".

The 1989 protest rested on absence. The nominees with the most at stake in the upcoming award chose not to appear for it.

Sinéad O'Connor boycotted the 1991 Grammy Awards and declined the trophy she won there. The Irish singer objected to the commercialism of the awards and of the music business behind them. She made her position public before the ceremony.

Recent findings suggest that the nominations came from her second studio album, I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got. It was released in 1990 and reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200. Its best-known track was "Nothing Compares 2 U." Prince wrote the song, and The Family, a group from his circle, first recorded it in 1985. O'Connor's version topped the singles charts in the U.S. and the U.K.

The album earned her several nominations at the 33rd Grammy Awards. They included Record of the Year for "Nothing Compares 2 U." That award went to Phil Collins for "Another Day in Paradise." She won Best Alternative Music Performance for the album. The Recording Academy introduced that category in 1991. O'Connor was its first winner.

In a recent development, she did not attend the ceremony and did not accept the award. Her refusal therefore had two parts. She stayed away from the event, and she turned down the prize itself.

Industry observers note that the refusal did not change the result. Voters had already chosen her, and the win remains in the Recording Academy's records.

According to recent reports, her complaint was wider than a dispute over a single category or a voting procedure. She objected to what the Grammys valued as a whole. In her view, that was commercial success.

The boycott fit a pattern from the same period. In August 1990, she stated she would not perform at a New Jersey concert if the U.S. national anthem was played beforehand. That stance drew wide criticism. In October 1992, she tore up a photograph of Pope John Paul II on NBC's Saturday Night Live. The act brought lasting backlash.

O'Connor died in July 2023 at 56. Her protest came after a win, not after a snub.

In a recent development, frank Ocean kept his 2016 album Blonde out of the running for the 2017 Grammys by choosing not to submit it. In a 2016 interview with The New York Times, he mentioned the institution did not seem to represent people who came from where he came from.

Ocean was not an outsider to the awards. At the 2013 Grammys, his debut studio album Channel Orange earned him six nominations, including Album of the Year, Record of the Year and Best Latest Artist. He won two. One was Best Urban Contemporary Album. The other was Best Rap/Sung Collaboration, for "No Church in the Wild" with Jay-Z and Kanye West. The Recording Academy had already honored the artist who later stayed out of its process.

Recent findings suggest that blonde also arrived just after Ocean finished his major-label deal. In August 2016, he released the visual album Endless through Def Jam. That release completed his contract with the label. A day later, he put out Blonde independently through his own Boys Don't Cry imprint. Apple $AAPL Music was its first streaming outlet.

Blonde debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. Its release date also fell inside the eligibility window for the 2017 ceremony, which ran from October 1, 2015, to September 30, 2016. On timing alone, it could have competed.

No entry was filed, so the album never went before the Academy's voters. Ocean's protest involved no stage moment and no confrontation at the ceremony itself.

In the Times interview, Ocean mentioned the institution "certainly has nostalgic importance." He paired that with the view that it was not representing people with his background well. He also compared his decision to Colin Kaepernick's protest. He said he would rather have that kind of moment than sit in the audience.

In a recent development, kaepernick was then the quarterback of the San Francisco 49ers. In 2016, he began kneeling during the national anthem before NFL games to protest police brutality and racial injustice.

The 2017 ceremony went ahead without Blonde in contention. Adele's 25 won Album of the Year that night.

It has been revealed that the Weeknd said in March 2021 that he would no longer let his label submit his music to the Grammys. The decision followed a shutout. His album After Hours received no nominations for the 2021 awards, and he blamed the Recording Academy's secret nomination committees.

Recent findings suggest that after Hours came out in March 2020. Its single "Blinding Lights" reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 that spring. When the Academy declared nominations in November 2020, The Weeknd did not appear in any category.

He responded on Twitter $TWTR. "The Grammys remain corrupt. You owe me, my fans and the industry transparency," he wrote.

The Weeknd was not upcoming to Grammy success. He had won Best Urban Contemporary Album for Beauty Behind the Madness at the 2016 ceremony. He won the same category again for Starboy at the 2018 ceremony. His complaint concerned how one year's nominees were chosen, not a career of being ignored.

In a March 2021 interview with The Latest York Times, he turned the tweet into a standing policy. "Because of the secret committees, I will no longer allow my label to submit my music to the Grammys," he told the paper. He was not skipping a single ceremony. He was taking his work out of the process.

It has been revealed that under the system he targeted, Academy members voted first. Anonymous review panels then examined the leading vote-getters in many categories and settled the final nominees. Panel members were not publicly identified, so outsiders could not see why a record made the cut or missed it.

On April 30, 2021, the Recording Academy said it would end those review committees in most categories. The change removed the specific mechanism The Weeknd had named.

It has been revealed that the dispute ran alongside one of his most visible bookings. He headlined the Super Bowl LV halftime show in February 2021, weeks before the Grammy ceremony in March.

Industry observers note that his method also differed from Sinéad O'Connor's in 1991. She turned down a Grammy after winning it, while The Weeknd chose not to compete at all.

Billionaire and longtime Bitcoin (BTC) supporter Tim Draper predicts a future where Bitcoin absorbs the innovations of other altcoins.

Draper's statement has major implications for massive cryptocurrencies like XRP, Ethereum (ETH) and Dogecoin (DOGE), which have built their own ecosystems and now compete in the wider cryptocurrency market.

In a recent post on X, Draper compared Bitcoin's rising dominance to Microsoft's path to becoming the dominant software company, as the company absorbed successful innovations from other businesses.

"Microsoft never invented the spreadsheet, word processor, or slide deck. They absorbed them," stated Draper.

The billionaire investor brought up pioneering software like Lotus 1-2-3 and WordPerfect, which eventually saw their dominance give way to Microsoft's Excel and Word.

Draper predicts that this could apply to the cryptocurrency industry, as Bitcoin could become the ultimate absorber of innovations from alternative blockchain networks.

"Altcoins are the Lotus 1-2-3s and WordPerfects of this time," wrote Draper.

Smaller cryptocurrencies are thus essentially incubators for technological innovations that could eventually become part of the bigger Bitcoin ecosystem, according to Draper.

"They show that it works, then the innovation that pulls the strongest gets ported to the Bitcoin platform," he added.

Draper also supported his statement by citing the rising market share of Bitcoin in the overall cryptocurrency market.

The billionaire investor recalled observing how Bitcoin dominance rose from about 40% to 50% and then even further to 61%.

"Bitcoin is that platform," said Draper, claiming that the biggest cryptocurrency could follow a path similar to Microsoft's.

This statement has implications for the future of significant altcoins like Ethereum, XRP and Dogecoin.

Ethereum is the leading smart contract and dApp platform, while XRP is mainly known for its cross-border payments and the wider XRP Ledger ecosystem. Meanwhile, Dogecoin is one of the most iconic meme coins in the cryptocurrency market.

Still, the growing ecosystem around Bitcoin, which adds more scaling and programmability through solutions such as the Lightning Network and projects like Stacks, shows how Bitcoin is trying to expand beyond its basic use case as a cryptocurrency.

  • These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”.

Instead, the Copilot as “a fresh OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

It has been revealed that microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

According to recent reports, many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the manufacturer’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

It has been revealed that the high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide consumers with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the upcoming Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The Fresh OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

According to recent reports, right now, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

According to recent reports, if you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, consumers don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

Recent findings suggest that “We increasingly think of all our apps together as a fresh operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

In a recent development, the end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella noted.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.
