What is the Recording Academy? This guide explains the U.S. nonprofit behind the Grammy Awards, from its 1957 founding and member voting to MusiCares and the Latin Grammys.

Plenty of television viewers know the Grammy trophy on sight. Far fewer know the organization that hands it out. That organization is the Recording Academy, and it works mostly out of view for the rest of the year. Knowing how it operates explains a lot about the Grammys — who picks the winners, why the rules change and what the Academy does between ceremonies.

So what is the Recording Academy? Its formal name is the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences. It is a U.S. nonprofit membership organization made up of people who make records for a living. Its members include performers, songwriters, producers and engineers. The Grammy Awards are its best-known program, but they are only one part of what the Academy does.

Industry observers note that the distinction matters most at voting time. Grammy winners are not decided by chart position, sales or streaming numbers. They are chosen by the Academy's voting members. That makes the Grammys an award given by peers. When an artist criticizes the Grammys, or when the Academy rewrites its nomination rules, the questions center on how a professional membership body runs itself.

The Academy's work also extends well beyond a single awards night. It runs charitable and educational programs connected to music. A museum bearing the Grammy name operates alongside it. It lobbies federal lawmakers in Washington, D.C., on issues that affect music creators. A separate sister organization runs a parallel awards show for Latin music.

Industry observers note that its history adds context. The Academy dates to the late 1950s. Its top leadership changed hands more than once in 2019 and 2020. Its awards process has also faced a public boycott by a major artist.

The 10 slides below take each piece in turn. They cover the Academy's origins and its first ceremony, who belongs and how members are organized, and how nominations and final voting work. They also explain the trophy's design and the four top awards in the General Field. The final slides cover the Latin Recording Academy, the Grammy Museum, the Academy's charities and its record on advocacy and governance. Each slide stands on its own, so readers looking for one answer can go straight to it.

In a recent development, the Recording Academy is a U.S. nonprofit organization of music professionals, and it is the group that runs the Grammy Awards. Its formal name is the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, though it generally goes by the shorter name.

People often use the two names interchangeably, but they refer to different things. The Recording Academy is the organization. The Grammy Awards are a program it operates, and they are its best-known one. Keeping the two apart makes it easier to follow how decisions about the awards get made.

Industry observers note that the Academy is a membership body made up of people who work in recorded music. Its members include performers, songwriters, producers and engineers. Performers are the singers and instrumentalists heard on a recording. Songwriters create the music and lyrics. Producers guide how a recording comes together, from arrangement choices to its final sound. Engineers handle the technical work of capturing and mixing audio.

Sources indicate that that range shapes what the organization represents. It speaks for the people who make recordings, not only the artists whose names appear on them. Many of its members work behind the scenes and are rarely seen by the public.

Recent findings suggest that its nonprofit status separates it from record labels, streaming services and other music companies. A nonprofit has no shareholders and does not pay out profits to owners. The Academy functions as a professional association, not as a business that sells music.

In a recent development, the distinction has practical consequences for anyone reading music news. When a report says the Recording Academy changed a rule or added a category, it describes a decision by the organization. The televised Grammy ceremony is the public face of that work, but the Academy operates year-round.

According to recent reports, the longer formal name still appears in official contexts. Either name refers to the same body: the U.S. peer organization of music professionals that stands behind the Grammy trophy.

Recent findings suggest that the Recording Academy was founded in 1957 by figures in the Los Angeles music business. It held its first Grammy Awards ceremony on May 4, 1959, honoring recordings from 1958.

The Academy existed for about two years before it handed out a single trophy.

It has been revealed that the first ceremony took place in two cities. The Academy held events on the same date in Beverly Hills, in the Los Angeles area, and in New York.

Recent findings suggest that the awards that night looked back a full year. Every recording honored at the 1959 ceremony came from 1958.

Sources indicate that one song won two of the night's major prizes. Domenico Modugno's "Nel Blu Dipinto Di Blu (Volare)" won Record of the Year. The same song also won Song of the Year.

Album of the Year went to a different winner. Henry Mancini took the award for The Music from Peter Gunn.

Modugno and Mancini are the first names in the Grammy record books. Every ceremony since 1959 has added to the list of winners that began with them.

It has been revealed that the Recording Academy's members are working music professionals, and they form the pool from which Grammy voters are drawn. Those members are organized through regional chapters in U.S. music hubs, including Los Angeles, Nashville and Fresh York.

In a recent development, membership is built around the people who make recordings. Performers belong alongside songwriters. Producers belong alongside the engineers who capture and shape sound in the studio. Several people credited on the same hit record can all be members of the same organization.

That structure makes the Academy a peer group. It is not a fan club, and it is not a trade body for record labels. The people who judge a piece of work come from the same trades as the people who made it. A songwriter's work is weighed by other songwriters and by the performers, producers and engineers who work with songwriters.

In a recent development, voting membership is tied to professional work in recorded music. Buying concert tickets or following an artist does not make someone eligible. The Academy sets its own rules for who qualifies. The line it draws separates people who work on records from people who listen to them.

According to recent reports, regional chapters give members a local base. The U.S. recording business is spread across several cities rather than concentrated in one. A chapter connects members with peers who work in the same city.

According to recent reports, the chapter system means a session engineer in Nashville and a producer in Los Angeles can belong to the same national organization. Each still has a chapter closer to home. Grouping members by city organizes the membership locally. It does not divide the Academy into separate regional organizations.

Sources indicate that the answer to who votes on the Grammys follows from this setup. The electorate is the Academy's professional membership, grouped by region. It is not the general public, and it is not a panel of critics.

Grammy winners are picked by the Recording Academy's voting members, not by sales charts or streaming totals. The vote happens in two stages: a nominations round that sets the field of contenders, then a final voting round that decides the winners.

Sources indicate that that design ties each result to the judgment of peers in the music business. A record can spend months at the top of the charts and still miss a nomination. A release with modest sales can still take home a trophy.

The nominations round comes first. Voting members cast ballots to narrow the eligible releases down to a set of nominees in each category. Those names are then confirmed as the year's Grammy nominees.

Industry observers note that the final voting round follows. Members vote again, this time choosing only among the declared nominees. The result of that second ballot decides who receives the trophy at the ceremony.

The two rounds are separate decisions with separate outcomes. The final ballot lists only the nominees. A release that misses the shortlist in the first round has no path to a win in the second. Each nominee also starts the final round on equal footing, whatever its sales or streaming record.

The process changed in 2021. That year, the Academy ended its anonymous nominations review committees. The change applied to the nominations stage, the first of the two rounds.

For listeners reading the results, the two-round structure offers a practical guide. A nomination highlights that the work drew enough support from voting members to reach the shortlist. A win shows that it then came out ahead of its fellow nominees in a separate final vote.

The Grammy takes its name from the gramophone, and the trophy is a gilded miniature of one. The award's name and its physical form both point to the same object: a machine built to play recorded sound.

"Grammy" is a shortened form of the word gramophone. The nickname ties the award to recorded music. Recorded work is the field the Recording Academy covers, and it is what the awards honor.

It has been revealed that the statuette carries the same reference in physical form. A winner does not receive an abstract figure or a plaque. The prize is a scaled-down gramophone.

Recent findings suggest that the pairing gives the award one consistent identity. The word read out during the broadcast and the object handed to a winner describe the same thing. A viewer who sees the trophy on stage is looking at a model of the device the name refers to.

The General Field holds the four top Grammy Awards: Album of the Year, Record of the Year, Song of the Year and Best Latest Artist. Two of them, Record of the Year and Song of the Year, are easy to confuse but reward different people.

The Recording Academy sorts its Grammy categories into groups called fields. Each field gathers related categories under one heading. The General Field is the group that contains the top awards.

Song of the Year honors the songwriters of a track. The award is about the composition — the words and music as they were written. A composition stays the same no matter who performs it. Its writers are the people this award recognizes.

Recent findings suggest that record of the Year honors the recording itself. Its credit covers the performers, producers and engineers who made that specific version of the track. The award recognizes how a piece of music was performed and captured. That credit places producers and engineers, who usually work behind the scenes, among the people honored in a top category.

Industry observers note that the split exists because a song and a recording are not the same thing. A songwriter who never sings on a track can still be honored for Song of the Year. A performer who did not write the track can still be credited for Record of the Year. One track can compete in both categories. Each award then goes to a different group of people.

Album of the Year covers a full album rather than a single track. Best Fresh Artist honors an artist rather than a specific piece of work. That makes it the only one of the four built around a person instead of a recording or composition.

Read together, the four General Field awards look at music on different scales: one written song, one recorded performance, one complete album and one artist's emergence.

Recent findings suggest that the Latin Recording Academy is a sister organization to the Recording Academy, with its own base in Miami and its own members. It runs the Latin Grammy Awards, which were first held in 2000.

The two groups share the Grammy name, but they are separate bodies. The Latin Recording Academy keeps a membership of its own, apart from the Recording Academy's.

That split determines who picks the winners. Latin Grammy voters come from the Latin Recording Academy's membership. They are not drawn from the members who vote on the main Grammy Awards.

In a recent development, the Latin Grammys are a distinct awards program. They are not a category or a field inside the Grammys, and each show holds its own ceremony.

A Latin Grammy and a Grammy come from two different member organizations. The Recording Academy runs the Grammys. The Latin Recording Academy runs the Latin Grammys from its Miami base.

The Grammy Museum opened in 2008 at L.A. Live in downtown Los Angeles. It operates alongside the Recording Academy, the nonprofit membership organization that runs the Grammy Awards.

Industry observers note that the museum and the awards are separate programs. The museum does not nominate recordings or choose winners. Those decisions belong to the Academy's voting members.

Sources indicate that the museum also runs on a different schedule from the awards. The Grammy ceremony happens once a year. A museum stays open between ceremonies. That gives the Grammy name a permanent public location.

Los Angeles was the first site. A second location opened eight years later. Grammy Museum Mississippi opened in 2016 in Cleveland, Mississippi.

The Mississippi site carries the state's name in its title. That name sets it apart from the original Los Angeles museum.

With both sites open, the Grammy Museum has locations in two U.S. states, California and Mississippi.

Industry observers note that musiCares is a nonprofit that provides health and human services to people who work in the music industry. The Recording Academy founded it in 1989.

According to recent reports, the Grammy Foundation is a separate nonprofit affiliated with the Academy. Its work centers on music education and music preservation.

MusiCares serves the people who make music, not the recordings they release. Its remit is health and human services. That places it outside the awards process. It does not nominate, judge or vote on anything.

Recent findings suggest that the charity was created 32 years after the Academy's 1957 founding. By 1989, the Academy had been presenting Grammys for three decades, dating back to the first ceremony in 1959.

The Grammy Foundation works on two fronts. Music education is about people learning music. Preservation is about keeping music that already exists from being lost.

The two charities split the Academy's nonprofit work by purpose. MusiCares deals with the needs of individuals in the music business. The Grammy Foundation deals with teaching music and safeguarding what has already been made.

In a recent development, neither organization picks Grammy winners or produces the Grammy telecast. Both operate as affiliated nonprofits alongside the Academy rather than as parts of its awards program.

Industry observers note that the Recording Academy lobbies in Washington as well as running the Grammys. It supported the Music Modernization Act, which became law in 2018. The Academy's leadership has also turned over since 2019, and in 2021 it ended its anonymous nominations review committees.

It has been revealed that advocacy is a separate job from the awards. The Academy's work in Washington is meant to serve the people who make recordings, whether or not they ever receive a nomination. When it presses federal lawmakers, it acts for the profession as a whole, not as the producer of a televised awards show. Its support for the Music Modernization Act is one example of that work.

It has been revealed that the Academy's top job has changed hands twice since 2019. Neil Portnow served as president and CEO from 2002 to 2019, a run of about 17 years. Deborah Dugan succeeded him as CEO. In January 2020, after about five months in the role, she was placed on leave.

Industry observers note that harvey Mason Jr. has led the Academy since 2020. Dugan's tenure, measured in months, was the shortest of the three. Portnow's, measured in years, was the longest. The two tenures sit at opposite ends of the Academy's recent history at the top.

According to recent reports, the 2021 end of the anonymous review committees came during Mason's time in charge. It was a decision about how the membership body runs its own selection process.

In 2021, The Weeknd publicly boycotted the Grammys. His boycott was widely reported and forms part of the public backdrop to that year's committee decision. A boycott of that kind is aimed at the institution that runs the awards, not at a single category.

According to recent reports, lobbying, leadership and the rules for choosing nominees all concern the Academy as an institution. None of them turns on a specific award or winner. Together they show the organization at work outside the annual ceremony it is best known for.

South Korea’s top scorer on the national tax accountant qualification exam has admitted to using AI to cheat.

Han Won-seok revealed in a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel that he used a small camera to photograph exam questions, sent the images to an AI tool, and checked the answers on his smartphone. He wore a face mask in the 14-minute long video, which has garnered more than 1.5 million views since being posted on Nov. 15.

Industry observers note that the Ministry of Economy and Finance will move to suspend Han’s qualifications. Under Korean law, candidates that cheat on their exam results are barred from taking the test again for five years, according to the Korea Herald.

South Korea’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin said during a committee meeting on Monday that the ministry would inspect every pair of glasses worn by students during this week’s national college entrance exams. Reuters reported that smart devices were added to a list of banned items in July.

Han acknowledged that his top ranking was fraudulent and apologized to fellow candidates, tax professionals, and exam officials. He also admitted to using the same method to cheat on a separate certified public accountant exam. “I deeply regret what I did,” Han mentioned.

Han said he is cooperating with authorities and would turn over his electronic equipment. He said he hoped an investigation might prevent similar incidents.

Asked by his lawyer why he cheated, Han mentioned he was worried about his future and wanted to make his parents proud. He said he later felt overwhelmed by guilt, particularly toward the runner up.

Han scored perfect scores in three of the four subjects tested in the exam, including in introductory tax law, a subject where most candidates got an average of score of just 30 points out of 100, according to the Korea Herald.

South Korea’s presidential office, Cheong Wa Dae, noted it was following the case “very seriously,” with the nationwide college entrance exam scheduled for Nov. 19, Yonhap News Agency reported.

Recent findings suggest that it’s not the country’s first brush with AI-assisted cheating. In October 2025, at least 40 students at Korea’s Yonsei University used ChatGPT and other AI tools to cheat during a midterm test, The Korea Herald reported. It said that an additional 10 students were suspected of using AI during the test.

In Japan, local media reported that an 18-year-old was referred to prosecutors after using smart glasses and recruiting tutors to help answer questions during a university entrance exam.

In June 2025, several AI providers including Tencent, Alibaba, Moonshot AI, and ByteDance suspended some functions during the gaokao, the make-or-break exam that governs where students go to university. The providers suspended features including photo recognition and question-answering.

Exams and education can become a flashpoint in Asia, where credentials can be critical for a successful career. In India, the leak of a medical entrance exam led to mass protests in New Delhi, forcing the education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that currencies such as the Japanese yen or the euro have tried and failed to loosen the U.S. dollar’s grip on world trade, unable to outweigh the U.S.’s deep and open financial markets. But now, Japanese bankers think that the rise of digital currencies could give the yen a newly introduced path to worldwide use.

“The currency competition is now a software competition,” Tomoya Hasebe, global head of digital and innovation at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), said at a roundtable organized by FinCity Tokyo in Singapore on Nov. 16. “Currency dominance is increasingly determined not only by central bank policy or regulatory policy, but by which currency is easiest to use as code.”.

Industry observers note that the yen is the world’s third most-used currency, after the U.S. dollar and the euro.

According to recent reports, japan was the first country among G7 economies to roll out a comprehensive framework to regulate stablecoins. Yet yen-pegged stablecoins have barely enjoyed much usage, with U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins accounting for more than 97% of the market.

The country’s three megabanks—Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, and the Mizuho Financial Group—are planning to change that with a jointly-issued yen-backed stablecoin set to begin transactions next March. The newly introduced stablecoin is meant to streamline cross-border payments and boost the appeal of the yen for global business.

Several Asian economies are rolling out their own stablecoins to cater to firms seeking alternatives to the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong, for example, issued its first two Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin issuer licenses in April, to HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture by Standard Chartered Bank, HKT, and Web3 firm Animoca Brands.

“The majority of global trade is still in USD, but there is certainly a group of firms around the world that want to not use U.S. dollars for trade,” said Tim Way, senior director of global banking at digital asset infrastructure firm Fireblocks. “It’s an opportunity for Asia to stand up and have more trade in Asia running in Asian currencies.”.

Industry observers note that startups are entering a financial ecosystem that’s long been dominated by incumbents. JPYC, a Japanese startup, launched the country’s first yen-pegged stablecoin in October 2025. “More private enterprises and start-ups are starting to enter the stablecoin area,” Makoto Shibata, the head of Finolab, a Japanese fintech accelerator, said.

Yet, it remains to be seen if yen-backed stablecoins—whether by on-chain start-ups or trad-fi institutions—will be able to gain traction. Unlike U.S. dollar stablecoins that generate returns from high-yielding treasury bills, yen-pegged stablecoins operate on razor-thin margins. Since JPYC was founded in 2019, it has faced steep growth bottlenecks, as people frequently redeem the token for traditional fiat, rather than hold it in their digital wallets.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Grammy eligibility window runs from late summer to late summer, which is why songs released last year often collect trophies at this year's ceremony.

  • In a recent development, the explanation sits in the calendar the Recording Academy uses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Grammy eligibility window runs from late summer to late summer, which is why songs released last year often collect trophies at this year's ceremony.

Recent findings suggest that A Grammy handed out in February usually rewards music that came out the year before. The trophy carries one year's date, while the songs behind it often belong to the previous one. Release dates and trophy years can look out of sync as a result.

In a recent development, the explanation sits in the calendar the Recording Academy uses. Its eligibility period does not run from January to December. It opens on Aug. 31 or Sept. 1 and closes on Aug. 30 of the following year. Any album, single or track released inside those dates can compete at the next ceremony.

The second piece of the puzzle is naming. Each ceremony takes the year in which it is held, not the year in which its music was released. A show staged in early 2026 therefore honors work that reached listeners across parts of 2024 and 2025. The label points forward, while the music looks back.

Put those two rules together and the timing starts to make sense. A record released in the spring sits inside one window. It then waits through the fall nominations, and any trophies are handed out the following winter. A record released just after the summer cutoff faces a much longer wait. It rolls into the next cycle entirely.

According to recent reports, the Grammy eligibility window explains why a song can win a trophy many months after listeners first heard it. It also shapes the schedule between release and ceremony. After the window closes, the Recording Academy needs time for entries, screening, voting rounds and a nominations announcement.

It has been revealed that the 10 slides that follow are a selection of key rules and examples, not a complete rulebook. They define the eligibility period and explain its late-summer cutoff. They walk through the windows for the 2025 and 2026 ceremonies, along with the event calendar from nominations to the show. Recent winners, including Beyoncé's Cowboy Carter and Kendrick Lamar's "Not Like Us," show the rules in practice. The final slides cover releases that miss the cutoff and the pandemic years, when ceremony dates moved but the window logic held.

In a recent development, the Grammy Awards honor music released within a fixed eligibility period, not within a calendar year. That period runs from Aug. 31 or Sept. 1 through Aug. 30 of the following year.

Sources indicate that the Recording Academy, the organization behind the Grammys, sets the dates for each awards cycle. The opening day falls on either Aug. 31 or Sept. 1, depending on the cycle. The closing day is always Aug. 30.

Each cycle uses only one of those two start dates. The correct window for a given year is the one the academy sets for that cycle.

According to recent reports, A release date decides where a song or album lands. Its position within the window determines which awards cycle it belongs to.

Sources indicate that the year on a record's release does not settle the question alone. Two albums released in the same calendar year can belong to different Grammy cycles. The deciding factor is which side of the Aug. 30 close each one falls on.

Consider an album released in January and another released in December of the same year. The January album sits in a window that opened the previous late summer. The December album sits in a window that opened only months earlier. They share a release year but compete at different ceremonies.

Each window covers about a year of releases. Every ceremony draws its contenders from a single window. That pairing of one window with one ceremony is the basic unit of the Grammy calendar.

Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC.
  • One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins.
  • Industry observers note that loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path highlights how far the probing went.

One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Industry observers note that loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, claims user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

The loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction reveals a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

That arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale states its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

Sources indicate that the two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

It has been revealed that the loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

Industry observers note that the takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

Industry observers note that this looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem reveals pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the XRP Ledger (XRPL) will be delivering a major enhancement on Dec. 3, which will address the occasional sluggishness the blockchain network has been experiencing in recent weeks.

As stated in a recent XRP Ledger Operations announcement, the network will be rolling out its upcoming version 3.5.0, which will exclusively include technical improvements and bug fixes, such as a lasting fix for the relatively slow ledger closing times.

In a recent development, "XRPL version 3.5.0 will be on Dec 3. Just improvements/fixes, including a long-lasting fix for the occasional slow ledger close times," XRP Ledger Operations said.

The developers have informed customers that the interim fixes to help improve the situation have already been working effectively.

"Interim fixes already helped improve close times, and we are watching the network very closely," it added.

This is a critical advancement in improving the reliability of the XRP Ledger, a network widely used to process cryptocurrency payments, tokenization, and stablecoin transactions.

The latest improvement to the XRPL comes after the blockchain network suffered technical problems in October, when some ledgers were closing much slower than usual.

According to recent reports, the XRP Ledger usually closes new ledgers once every three to five seconds. This ensures that transaction confirmations happen fairly swiftly.

However, intermittent sluggishness was seen on the network, as XRP Ledger Operations admitted on Oct. 21. The team later confirmed that its developers were already working on the glitch.

Afterward, XRP Ledger Operations started sharing a recommended configuration revision for xrpld software with network operators such as validators and other infrastructure providers.

The temporary fixes were helpful. On Oct. 22, XRP Ledger Operations shared that the occasional slower ledger closures were no longer happening, thanks to the new recommended configuration.

That said, the developers remain hard at work to deliver a software fix that will correct the matter once and for all, a long-term solution that would not rely solely on temporary changes.

That is why the December release is expected to finally bring that permanent fix.

In the meantime, Vet, one of the notable XRP Ledger validators, has already assured the community that the blockchain network is always being monitored as developers work on more improvements.

In a recent post on X, he stressed that a great amount of work has been put into network monitoring, information security and engineering.

Vet stated that their engineers are always on call to address any possible incidents.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Anthropic goes public this week, several major players will enjoy a windfall after having snapped up shares at firesale prices in 2024 at the bankruptcy liquidation of collapsed crypto exchange FTX. Those include the quant giant Jane Street, which spent $1.34 billion to purchase Anthropic shares at the time—a stake that is likely to be worth over $35 million after the IPO. And, in a twist of fate, Jane Street is the first employer of Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced founder of FTX, who is now serving a 25-year sentence for fraud in federal prison.

Industry observers note that bankman-Fried expressed frustration over the sale in a recent interview with The Fresh York Times, criticizing the bankruptcy administrators who took control of FTX after its collapse. In addition to Jane Street, other buyers of FTX’s Anthropic shares are an investment vehicle linked to Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala and the Ford Foundation, both of which are also poised to share in the windfall.

Bankman-Fried became one of Anthropic’s earliest investors in late 2021, when he put $500 million into the little-known startup for a 13.5% stake that later shrank as the company raised more money, according to The Newly introduced York Times.

Sources indicate that nearly five years later, Anthropic is just two days away from pricing what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in history, with trading on the Nasdaq expected to begin Thursday. Its proposed price range of $70 to $78 per share would value the organization at up to roughly $1.4 trillion. The company behind the Claude chatbot generated $17 billion in revenue in the third quarter alone, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier, according to earlier Fortune reporting.

Bankman-Fried’s interest in the tech giant stemmed in part from his connections to its cofounder, former OpenAI executive Dario Amodei. The two moved in the same tech circles and shared concerns about the risks of powerful AI, according to the Times. Mutual acquaintances connected them shortly after Amodei left OpenAI to start Anthropic.

At the time of FTX’s investment into Anthropic, Bankman-Fried was also illegally using his customers’ money to make numerous other bets and spraying funds to several politicians in Washington, DC in a bid to gain political influence.

FTX, though, would not survive to see the  early bet on Anthropic mature. In November 2022, the exchange collapsed after a run on deposits exposed an $8 billion hole in customer accounts—a scandal that ultimately led to Bankman-Fried’s conviction on fraud and conspiracy charges and a hefty prison sentence.

In a recent development, the bankruptcy administrators who took control sold the Anthropic shares in 2024 to raise money to repay customers. By then, Anthropic had rolled out Claude and attracted billions of dollars from investors, including Amazon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A Bitcoin (BTC) address from 2010 has become active after being dormant for over 16 years.
  • According to blockchain tracking platform Whale Alert, the address held 50 BTC, which was roughly equivalent to $3,442,939 at the time of activation.
  • Recent findings suggest that the dormant address had been inactive for 16.2 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A Bitcoin (BTC) address from 2010 has become active after being dormant for over 16 years. The address has transferred around $3.4 million in BTC.

According to blockchain tracking platform Whale Alert, the address held 50 BTC, which was roughly equivalent to $3,442,939 at the time of activation.

Recent findings suggest that the dormant address had been inactive for 16.2 years. Back in BTC's early days, all 50 BTC were worth just $3.

Notably, this wasn’t the only old Bitcoin address that suddenly became active.

According to Whale Alert, another dormant Bitcoin address holding 50 BTC worth roughly $3,442,129 became active after 16.2 years.

The address became active with 50 BTC.

Recent findings suggest that the two transfers took place within minutes of each other on Nov. 13. Hence, the total value of the newly activated Bitcoin comes to around $6.89 million.

According to recent reports, there’s no confirmation about who owned these wallets. Also, it’s not confirmed if the same individual or entity owns these addresses.

The reason these addresses are significant is that they date back to 2010, which is considered to be the Satoshi era.

In simple terms, the Satoshi era refers to the first few years of Bitcoin, mainly 2009 and 2010. During those years, the pseudonymous founder of Bitcoin, Satoshi Nakamoto, was pretty active in the network's development.

To be precise, Bitcoin came into existence in January 2009. It initially carried a block reward of 50 BTC. This block reward of 50 BTC continued until Bitcoin had its first halving in November 2012.

This is why these newly activated addresses’ holdings of 50 BTC match the rewards miners could receive during the early days of Bitcoin.

These old addresses always raise a lot of interest as Bitcoin had relatively few miners and consumers during those times.

However, this does not mean that these wallets are owned by the mysterious founder of Bitcoin.

According to recent reports, this recent activation comes after a series of interesting activations in the crypto world. These are long-dormant crypto addresses that have become active over the past month.

Recent findings suggest that on Oct. 22, a Bitcoin address with 170 BTC worth roughly $14.38 million became active after being dormant for 13 years, as reported by Whale Alert.

Sources indicate that prior to this, on Oct. 20, a dormant address with 500 BTC worth around $41.54 million became active after 10.7 years. In 2016, these holdings were worth just $194,955.

Later, crypto analytics platform Arkham linked the 500 BTC transaction to addresses belonging to convicted Irish drug dealer Clifton Collins. Previously, his crypto holdings were deemed inaccessible.

On Oct. 17, Whale Alert tracked activity involving old Bitcoin addresses holding 248 BTC and 167 BTC worth roughly $20.24 million and $13.65 million, respectively.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian thinks Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop came from “a combination of faulty equipment, coupled with human error.” He dismissed other explanations as at the moment lacking evidence.
  • Bastian, speaking with Fortune’s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, said he has no information beyond what has been reported.
  • The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, canceling roughly 12,500 flights that day and thousands more on Saturday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian thinks Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop came from “a combination of faulty equipment, coupled with human error.” He dismissed other explanations as at the moment lacking evidence. “There’s no evidence that there’s [an] AI trigger. There’s no evidence that there’s cyber at play.”.

Bastian, speaking with Fortune’s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, said he has no information beyond what has been reported. “We’ll find out when it comes in,” he said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, canceling roughly 12,500 flights that day and thousands more on Saturday. It was the first nationwide stop since a January 2023 system outage, and only the second since 9/11.

In a recent development, bastian noted he has talked to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and that Duffy “has been very transparent.” Duffy has said the trouble started during a copper-to-fiber switch at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Ark. A router at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, then “started to flood our system.” Contractor L3Harris did the installation, and Duffy has asked publicly whether the fault was the install or the router itself. L3Harris says it is supporting the investigation. Bedford said there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related.”.

Bastian said the router work wasn’t new. “I think they’ve replaced, I understand, close to 70% of the routers already,” he said. L3Harris indicates the switch to fiber is more than 70% done. “So I don’t know. I can’t explain it.”.

He said the system came back once the routers were taken offline, but finding them “took hours.” He put the cost of the disruption “in the billions.”.

Asked if more nationwide stops are coming, he called Friday “clearly an anomaly” and said he wouldn’t extrapolate “until we know what happened.”.

It has been revealed that bastian used the outage to argue for spending. Investors are putting “hundreds of billions, if not trillions of dollars” into AI and data centers, he stated, but “we can’t even get $50 billion to fix our skies.” Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control last year. Duffy has said he wants $50 billion on top of that. President Trump has asked for $30 billion.

“The terrible thing would be if we use this instance to ‘lose confidence in what we’re doing,” Bastian said.

It has been revealed that he also pointed out that it takes longer to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia today than it did when Delta rolled out the route in the 1950s. He said more capacity in the skies is the only way to lower fares. “We’re congested, we’re gridlocked.”.

Industry observers note that bastian stated Delta’s profit this year will be “pretty similar” to last year’s despite a $6 billion jump in its fuel bill. Delta’s ticket prices are up 15% to 20% year-over-year, he remarked with amazement: “We have never seen that dramatic growth.” Delta’s adjusted revenue rose 16% in the third quarter, and the organization expects about 20% growth in the fourth.

Delta could either raise prices or cut flights, he stated, arguing that “people are willing to pay more rather than have their options limited.” Most of its customers, he said, live “in the upper end of the K” and want to spend on travel, he said, referring to what economists call the “K-shaped economy.”.

Shontell noted that a planned Delta route to Riyadh, first revealed at the Fortune Global Forum in October 2025, was pushed back after missile attacks on the Riyadh airport. Bastian said service hadn’t started yet when the airport was hit.

Recent findings suggest that shontell also asked about Elon Musk, who has been going after Delta on X since the airline picked Amazon’s Leo satellite service over SpaceX’s Starlink. In early October, Musk posted that Bastian “will lose his job over this” and that “Delta will lose a lot of customers.” He also joked that a Delta flight was a good place to sandbox an AI model because there’s no internet. Delta revealed the Amazon deal in March. Leo is slated for 500 Delta planes starting in 2028. United is already installing Starlink across its fleet.

Recent findings suggest that bastian remarked Delta “helped them get started in aviation,” giving SpaceX planes to test on during COVID. “We just couldn’t come to an agreement on a business model.” He said customers don’t pick airlines based on Wi-Fi, and that when Leo arrives, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink, if not better.”.

Sources indicate that leo has a new problem, though. On Sunday, a United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit and lost all 40 Amazon Leo satellites it was carrying. Amazon had about 400 in orbit before the launch.

In a recent development, on AI, Bastian stuck to his line that the technology is there to help Delta’s roughly 100,000 workers, not replace them. “I’m not getting on any planes operated by AI with one pilot,” he noted. Bastian previously told Fortune that he hates the phrase AI and prefers to use “augmented intelligence” instead.

Sources indicate that customers who call about the AI never praise it, he noted. “They always complain about the AI.” The biggest issue with AI in the U.S. is trust, he said. Workers whose jobs change will be moved “to the extent capable into service, at airports or on the phones.

What is an EGOT? 10 stars who've won an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meet 10 EGOT winners who earned an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony, and learn what the rare entertainment grand slam means and what each star won.
  • An EGOT means one person has won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony.
  • Industry observers note that only competitive wins count toward the title.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meet 10 EGOT winners who earned an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony, and learn what the rare entertainment grand slam means and what each star won.

An EGOT means one person has won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony. Each of those four awards covers a different part of the entertainment business. Emmys go to television, Grammys to recorded music, Oscars — formally the Academy Awards — to film, and Tonys to Broadway theater. Collecting all four requires success in fields with separate audiences, separate production systems and separate voters.

Industry observers note that only competitive wins count toward the title. An honorary award does not complete the set. That rule keeps the group small. It also explains why some performers with shelves of trophies still fall outside it. An artist can lead one field for decades and never earn a qualifying win in another.

Sources indicate that the routes to the milestone vary. Some winners are composers and songwriters whose work moved between the stage, the screen and the recording studio. Others are actors who added a Grammy for a spoken-word recording or an audiobook to their acting honors. Producing credits count too. Jennifer Hudson completed her set in 2022 with a Tony as a producer of A Strange Loop.

According to recent reports, the timeline stretches across more than 60 years. Richard Rodgers is generally recorded as the first person to complete an EGOT, finishing in 1962. Rita Moreno and Helen Hayes both completed their sets in 1977. John Legend finished his in 2018 and became the first Black man to reach the milestone. Viola Davis followed in 2023, and Elton John completed his set with an Emmy in 2024.

Sources indicate that this slideshow profiles 10 EGOT winners, a selection rather than the complete list or a ranking. Each slide sets out the four awards behind one person's set, with titles and years where the record is clear. The group includes film actors, a Broadway composer, a comedy writer and director, and pop musicians. Their wins span Broadway musicals, film dramas, live television concerts and audiobooks.

Industry observers note that richard Rodgers is generally recorded as the first person to win an EGOT. The Broadway composer completed the set in 1962, when he won an Emmy for his music for Winston Churchill: The Valiant Years.

The Emmy was the final piece. Rodgers had already won the other three awards through work in film, recorded music and the stage. Nearly all of it grew out of the same body of songwriting.

Recent findings suggest that his Oscar came first. Rodgers won the Academy Award for best original song for the 1945 film State Fair. The movie was a Hollywood musical with a score by Rodgers and his lyricist partner, Oscar Hammerstein II. It was the only musical the pair wrote directly for the screen.

It has been revealed that his Tony Awards came from Broadway, where he built his career. Rodgers wrote the music for a long list of stage shows. With Lorenz Hart, his first major collaborator, he wrote musicals including The Boys from Syracuse and Pal Joey.

In a recent development, with Hammerstein, he wrote Oklahoma!, Carousel, South Pacific, The King and I and The Sound of Music. South Pacific also earned Rodgers a share of the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. That fifth major honor places him in a smaller group sometimes called PEGOT winners.

Recent findings suggest that the Grammy traced back to the stage as well. Rodgers won it for the original cast album of The Sound of Music. Cast recordings carried Broadway scores to listeners who never saw the shows in a theater.

Sources indicate that the Emmy came from a different kind of project. Winston Churchill: The Valiant Years was a television documentary series about the British wartime prime minister. Rodgers composed music for it.

He had worked in documentary television before. Rodgers wrote the music for Victory at Sea, an NBC series from the early 1950s about naval combat in World War II.

It has been revealed that his later stage work changed after Hammerstein died in 1960. Rodgers wrote both the music and the lyrics for No Strings, which opened on Broadway in 1962 — the same year he completed his EGOT.

Rodgers was born in Fresh York City in 1902 and died in 1979.

In a recent development, helen Hayes completed her EGOT in 1977, when she won a Grammy for a spoken-word recording. By then she already held two Oscars, one for The Sin of Madelon Claudet and one for Airport. She also had Emmy and Tony wins from her television and stage work.

It has been revealed that her two film awards sit at opposite ends of a long career. The Sin of Madelon Claudet, released in 1931, earned her the Academy Award for best actress at the ceremony held in 1932. In the film she plays a woman who makes years of personal sacrifices to pay for her son's upbringing and education.

According to recent reports, airport brought her a second Oscar, for best supporting actress, at the ceremony held in 1971. She played Ada Quonsett, an elderly woman who sneaks onto flights as a stowaway. The two Oscar ceremonies took place 39 years apart.

Sources indicate that the theater was her main base. Hayes was born in Washington, D.C., in 1900 and began acting as a child. She became known as the "First Lady of the American Theatre." Her title role as Queen Victoria in Victoria Regina, which opened on Broadway in 1935, became one of her best-known stage performances.

Her Tony record reaches back to the start of the awards. She won best actress in a play at the first Tony Awards in 1947 for Happy Birthday. She won a second Tony in 1958 for Time Remembered. The award is named for Antoinette Perry, a stage actress and director who died in 1946.

Television added the Emmy. She won the award for best actress in 1953, in the medium's early years, when much TV drama aired live.

In a recent development, the Grammy came last. It honored a spoken-word recording rather than music. She was 76 when the win arrived. It made her the second person to complete an EGOT, after composer Richard Rodgers.

Hayes died in 1993. A Broadway house on West 44th Street was renamed in her honor in 1983. It now operates as the Hayes Theater.

According to recent reports, rita Moreno completed her EGOT in 1977, when she won an Emmy. Her run began with an Oscar for West Side Story (1961). A Grammy followed in 1972, and a Tony came in 1975.

The Oscar recognized her performance as Anita in the film version of the Broadway musical. She won in the best supporting actress category. Moreno was born in Puerto Rico, and the win made her the first Latina actress to receive an Academy Award.

Recent findings suggest that her Grammy came from children's television rather than film or the stage. Moreno was a cast member on The Electric Company, a PBS series built to teach reading skills to young viewers. A recording tied to the show earned her the Grammy in 1972.

Sources indicate that broadway supplied the third award. Moreno won a Tony in 1975 for The Ritz, a Terrence McNally farce set in a Latest York bathhouse. She played Googie Gomez, a nightclub singer with large ambitions and limited talent. She returned to the role in the 1976 film version, directed by Richard Lester.

Recent findings suggest that television completed the set. Her 1977 Emmy came for a guest appearance on The Muppet Show. A year later, she won a second Emmy for The Rockford Files, the detective series starring James Garner.

The acronym lists the awards in a fixed sequence, but winners can collect them in any order. Moreno's sequence was Oscar, Grammy, Tony and then Emmy. Each came from a different kind of work: a film musical, a children's recording, a stage comedy and a network television guest spot.

Sources indicate that her honors extend beyond the four competitive awards. President George W. Bush presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2004. She has also received the National Medal of Arts, and she was a Kennedy Center honoree in 2015.

Sources indicate that west Side Story returned to her career decades later. Steven Spielberg's 2021 film adaptation cast her as Valentina, a character written for the fresh version. She also served as an executive producer on that film, 60 years after the original adaptation that won her the Oscar.

In a recent development, audrey Hepburn is an EGOT winner. She won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony.

All four of Hepburn's awards were competitive wins, which places her among the performers who hold the full set.

Mel Brooks is an EGOT winner whose Oscar and Tonys trace back to one story: The Producers. He won the Academy Award for the film's screenplay. He later won Tonys for the Broadway musical adaptation, which opened in 2001.

It has been revealed that brooks wrote and directed The Producers as a 1967 film comedy. It follows a failing Broadway producer and a timid accountant who scheme to profit from a guaranteed flop. Their chosen show is a musical called Springtime for Hitler. Zero Mostel and Gene Wilder played the two leads.

The film was Brooks's first feature as a director. His Oscar recognized the original screenplay he wrote for it. That made it a writing award rather than a directing or acting honor.

Sources indicate that brooks adapted the story for the stage decades later. He wrote the music and lyrics and co-wrote the book with Thomas Meehan. Nathan Lane and Matthew Broderick starred. Susan Stroman directed and choreographed the production.

According to recent reports, the Broadway production won 12 Tony Awards. No show has won more. Brooks took home Tonys of his own for his work on the musical. That tied the theater leg of his EGOT to the same title as his film award.

In a recent development, his Emmys come from television, a medium that shaped his early career. Brooks wrote for Sid Caesar's Your Show of Reveals in the 1950s. He later co-created the spy spoof Get Smart with Buck Henry. His Emmy wins include awards for guest appearances as Uncle Phil on the NBC sitcom Mad About You.

He also holds a Grammy, drawn from a long recording history in comedy. That body of work includes the 2000 Year Old Man routines he performed with Carl Reiner.

Recent findings suggest that brooks also made the film comedies Blazing Saddles and Young Frankenstein, both released in 1974. The Producers itself returned to movie screens in 2005. That year the stage musical was adapted into a film, with Lane and Broderick reprising their roles.

Whoopi Goldberg is an EGOT winner whose four competitive awards came from comedy recording, film acting, daytime television and Broadway producing. She won her Oscar for the 1990 film Ghost and completed the set in 2002.

The first of the four was a Grammy for recorded comedy. Goldberg won the 1986 Grammy for best comedy recording for the album of her one-woman Broadway show. Mike Nichols produced that show. It was a series of character monologues, and it introduced her to a national audience in the mid-1980s.

Recent findings suggest that her first major screen role came in the same period. She played Celie in Steven Spielberg's The Color Purple, released in 1985. The performance won her a Golden Globe for best actress in a drama. It also earned a best actress Oscar nomination, though she did not win that award.

Recent findings suggest that ghost brought the Academy Award. Goldberg played Oda Mae Brown, a fraudulent psychic who discovers she can hear a murdered man's spirit. Patrick Swayze and Demi Moore played the couple at the center of the story. The role won her the Oscar for best supporting actress, along with the Golden Globe in the same category. Ghost was also the highest-grossing film worldwide in 1990.

Industry observers note that that Oscar made her the second Black woman to receive an acting Oscar. The first was Hattie McDaniel, who won for Gone with the Wind.

The final two pieces of her EGOT arrived in the same year. Goldberg won a Daytime Emmy in 2002 for Beyond Tara: The Extraordinary Life of Hattie McDaniel, a documentary special she hosted. The film profiled the same actress whose Oscar had come before hers.

According to recent reports, she also won a Tony in 2002 as one of the producers of Thoroughly Modern Millie. The musical, starring Sutton Foster, took the Tony for best musical. That award goes to a show's producers. As a result, Goldberg's name went on a Broadway trophy without a performing credit.

According to recent reports, daytime television became a larger part of her career afterward. Goldberg became moderator of ABC's The View in 2007. In 2009, she and her co-hosts shared the Daytime Emmy for outstanding talk show host.

Sources indicate that john Legend completed his EGOT in 2018, when he won an Emmy as a producer of NBC's Jesus Christ Superstar Live in Concert. That win made him the first Black man to hold competitive Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards.

The Emmy was for outstanding variety special (live). NBC aired the production on Easter Sunday, April 1, 2018. Legend played Jesus in the live staging of the rock opera by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice. He was also one of its producers. That credit put his name on the Emmy. The award was presented at the Creative Arts Emmys in September 2018.

Lloyd Webber and Rice shared that same Emmy as producers. The award completed their EGOTs as well. Three people reached the milestone through a single award on the same night.

In a recent development, legend's path to the four awards began in music. He won the Grammy for best new artist in 2006, after the release of his debut album, Get Lifted. He added more Grammys in R&B categories in the years that followed.

It has been revealed that his Oscar came from film. Legend and Common shared the Academy Award for best original song for "Glory." They wrote it for Selma, Ava DuVernay's 2014 drama about the 1965 voting rights marches in Alabama. The Oscar was presented in February 2015.

According to recent reports, the Tony arrived in 2017. Legend was one of the producers of the Manhattan Theatre Club revival of August Wilson's Jitney. The production won the Tony for best revival of a play. Jitney belongs to Wilson's 10-play cycle about Black American life, with one play set in each decade of the 20th century. Its story follows drivers at an unlicensed cab station in Pittsburgh.

Two of Legend's four awards came through producing credits. The Tony and the Emmy both recognized his role in backing a production. His Grammy and Oscar recognized his own work as a singer and songwriter.

Jennifer Hudson completed her EGOT in 2022 with a Tony as a producer of the Broadway musical A Strange Loop. Her run of competitive wins began with an Oscar for Dreamgirls in 2007 and closed 15 years later.

It has been revealed that hudson first reached a national audience on American Idol in 2004. She finished seventh in the show's third season. Fantasia Barrino won that season. Hudson's major awards all came after that early exit.

The Oscar came for her first film role. In Dreamgirls, Hudson played Effie White, a singer pushed out of the lead spot in her own group. The film adapted the 1981 Broadway musical of the same name, and Bill Condon directed it. The Academy named her best supporting actress.

Her Grammy followed in 2009, two years after the Oscar. It went to her self-titled debut album, Jennifer Hudson, which won best R&B album. Its lead single was Spotlight.

Her other two awards came through producing rather than performing. Her Emmy was for Baba Yaga's Heart, a project she worked on as a producer. Her Tony came as one of the producers of A Strange Loop.

Sources indicate that A Strange Loop is a musical by Michael R. Jackson. It follows Usher, a young Black queer writer who works as a Broadway usher while trying to finish a musical of his own. The show won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 2020, before it opened on Broadway. It won the Tony for best musical in 2022.

On Broadway, the Tony for best musical is presented to the show's producers. Each credited producer can count that win toward an EGOT without appearing on stage.

Industry observers note that hudson has continued to work in film and television since her Oscar. She played Aretha Franklin in the 2021 biopic Respect. She also hosts The Jennifer Hudson Show, a daytime talk program that premiered in 2022.

Viola Davis completed her EGOT in 2023, when the audiobook of her memoir Finding Me won a Grammy. That win joined an Oscar, two Tonys and an Emmy she had already earned for acting.

The Grammy came in the best audio book, narration and storytelling recording category. Davis narrated Finding Me herself. The memoir, published in 2022, recounts her childhood in poverty in Central Falls, Rhode Island. It also traces her path into acting.

Her Oscar came for Fences, the 2016 film adaptation of August Wilson's play. Denzel Washington directed the film and played Troy Maxson. Davis played his wife, Rose, and won best supporting actress at the Academy Awards ceremony in 2017.

Fences also accounts for one of her Tonys. Davis played Rose in the 2010 Broadway revival, again opposite Washington. That performance won her the Tony for best leading actress in a play.

Sources indicate that her first Tony came nine years earlier, for King Hedley II, another Wilson drama. That 2001 award was for best featured actress in a play. Both Tony-winning roles come from Wilson's cycle of 10 plays. Each play in the cycle is set in a different decade of the 20th century and depicts Black American life.

Recent findings suggest that television supplied the Emmy. Davis won outstanding lead actress in a drama series in 2015 for How to Get Away with Murder. She played Annalise Keating, a law professor and defense attorney, in the ABC legal drama. Davis was the first Black woman to win that Emmy category.

Industry observers note that the 2017 Oscar gave her competitive acting awards from film, television and Broadway. That combination is often called the Triple Crown of Acting. Davis was the first Black performer to complete it.

The Grammy arrived six years after the Oscar and turned that acting triple crown into a full EGOT. Every award in her set recognizes her work as a performer. Her Emmy, Oscar and Tonys honored characters she played. The Grammy honored her reading of her own life story.

Elton John completed his EGOT in 2024, when Elton John Live: Farewell from Dodger Stadium won an Emmy. That television win joined the Oscar, Tony and Grammy awards he had already won.

The special captured the final North American concert of his Farewell Yellow Brick Road tour. The show took place at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in November 2022 and streamed live on Disney $DIS+. The venue had history for him. He played two sold-out reveals there in October 1975, a run remembered for the sequined Dodgers uniform he wore on stage.

The program won in the outstanding variety special (live) category at the Creative Arts Emmys in September 2024. The award went to the special's producers, and John was among them. A producing win is a competitive Emmy. It counts toward the four-award set.

His first Oscar came from animation. "Can You Feel the Love Tonight," written with lyricist Tim Rice for Disney's The Lion King, won best original song at the Academy Awards in March 1995. He won a second Oscar in the same category in 2020. That one was for "(I'm Gonna) Love Me Again," written with his longtime lyricist Bernie Taupin for the biopic Rocketman.

It has been revealed that broadway supplied the Tony. John and Rice wrote the score for Aida, a stage musical built on the story of Giuseppe Verdi's opera. The show opened on Broadway in 2000 and won the Tony for best original score that year.

In a recent development, his Grammy wins include one for "Candle in the Wind 1997." The track reworked his 1973 song "Candle in the Wind," with new lyrics by Taupin, as a tribute to Diana, Princess of Wales. John performed it at her funeral at Westminster Abbey in September 1997. The recording won the Grammy for best male pop vocal performance in 1998.

It has been revealed that television was the last of the four categories he needed. The Emmy arrived 24 years after his Tony for Aida. It also came from a filmed concert rather than an acting role or a scripted series. His EGOT rests on songwriting for film and stage, a pop vocal recording and a live performance broadcast to a streaming audience.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that savings matter.
  • It has been revealed that across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every CEO I talk to has an AI savings plan. Almost none have an AI revenue plan.

It has been revealed that savings matter. But an AI strategy that stops there is incomplete.

It has been revealed that across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies. I’ve watched successive technology waves play out the same way. The first instinct is to use the newly introduced tool to do the old things cheaper. The companies that win use it to do new things. Electricity didn’t just lower factory power bills; it let factories be rebuilt around the assembly line. The internet didn’t just cut the cost of mailing catalogs; it created Amazon.

An EY-Parthenon survey published in April 2026 found that 63% of growth leaders at large U.S. companies said their organizations were using AI primarily for efficiency and productivity. The hard part remains choosing the right opportunities, validating demand, and turning them into viable businesses. Every established company has expertise in how its industry actually works. Customer knowledge: what people complain about, ask for, pay extra for, and work around. Capabilities built for one purpose that could serve another. Some also have patents, trade secrets, or research shelved because building on them was too expensive to staff. Open it to more people. Cut the cost of a premium service so a new customer group can afford it. What would that make possible?

Get the timing right. Look for a falling cost curve, a platform shift, or a regulatory change. Exhume the graveyard: revisit projects shelved because they were right but too early.

Think big. Reimagine a giant but static industry, or start from a bold vision of a better future.

Consider a logistics company that can predict delivery disruptions. Could that expertise support a planning service for smaller shippers? AI can help explore the possibility. Customers still need to demonstrate that the problem matters enough to pay for a solution.

According to recent reports, run these lenses against your expertise, customer knowledge, capabilities, and intellectual property. Use customer interviews, prototypes, or paid pilots to learn what people actually need and whether they will pay. What does 007 mean? The 00 license to kill, explained
