📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here's what 007 means, how James Bond's double-0 code number and fictional license to kill work in Ian Fleming's novels and films, and how real U.K.
  • The number 007 is a job code, not a name.
  • Bond is the fictional MI6 officer created by the British novelist Ian Fleming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here's what 007 means, how James Bond's double-0 code number and fictional license to kill work in Ian Fleming's novels and films, and how real U.K. law compares.

The number 007 is a job code, not a name. It is James Bond's service number. It tells the reader which section Bond belongs to and what that section authorizes him to do. That is why the question "what does 007 mean" has a precise answer, and that answer starts in the original novels.

Bond is the fictional MI6 officer created by the British novelist Ian Fleming. MI6 is the common name for the Secret Intelligence Service, the U.K.'s foreign intelligence agency. Fleming introduced his agent in the novel Casino Royale, published in 1953. Eon Productions released its first Bond film, Dr. No, in 1962, with Sean Connery in the lead role. The code number moved with the character from page to screen.

The number has two parts. The double zero marks a special section, and the final digit identifies one officer within it. In Fleming's fiction, the prefix carries an authority that ordinary officers do not hold. It is the authority to kill in the line of duty, known in shorthand as the license to kill. Both the section and the license are inventions of the stories, not features of the real MI6.

According to recent reports, this guide works through the code one piece at a time. It covers how the prefix is read, how Bond earned it in the original novel and how the 2006 film of the same name retold that moment. It looks at the other double-0 agents who appear on screen and at the film that handed the 007 number to someone new. It also explains the real U.K. law that comes closest to a license to kill, and why that law is something else entirely. The final slide turns to Fleming's wartime work in British naval intelligence and the 1989 film that borrowed the phrase for its title.

Each slide stands on its own, so readers can start with whichever part of the 007 question they need.

007 is James Bond's service number, the code that identifies him inside MI6 in Ian Fleming's spy novels. The double zero places him in a special section, and the closing seven singles him out as one agent within it.

Recent findings suggest that the code works like an address. The first two characters point to the unit. The last character points to one officer inside that unit.

Industry observers note that that makes 007 a designation rather than a name. It describes a position within an organization, and Bond is the man who fills it. Both the officer and his section exist only in fiction, not in the real MI6.

Sources indicate that the number arrived on the page with the character in Casino Royale, Fleming's first Bond novel. Dr. No, the first Eon Productions film, later carried both to cinemas with Sean Connery in the role.

Fleming never gave a documented reason for choosing seven. No statement from the author explains why Bond received that digit rather than another. Theories about its origin circulate, but none rests on anything Fleming verifiably remarked or wrote.

The digit's job inside the stories is clearer than its origin. It tells one double-0 officer apart from the others in the same section. Nothing in the code itself says more than that.

In Ian Fleming's James Bond novels, the double-0 prefix marks an officer of the double-0 section. Officers in that section are authorized to kill in the line of duty. "License to kill" is the shorthand for that authority.

The prefix and the license work as a pair. The double-0 number is the marker. The authority to kill is what that marker signals.

According to recent reports, the phrase describes a power rather than a formal rank or job title. It compresses what the prefix permits into three words.

Recent findings suggest that the authority is tied to the line of duty. In the fiction, it covers what a double-0 officer does on assignment for the service.

Industry observers note that fleming introduced the idea in Casino Royale, the novel that rolled out the series. In that book, Bond reflects on his double-0 status and on what the authority to kill means for him. The license enters the series in the same book as the character himself.

Industry observers note that the double-0 section carries over into the Eon Productions films. On screen, as in the novels, the license works as a plot device.

It has been revealed that both the section and its powers are story devices. Fleming built them into his invented version of MI6. They exist only on the page and on screen.

Recent findings suggest that james Bond earns his double-0 prefix in Ian Fleming's 1953 novel Casino Royale by killing two people on assignment. The 2006 film of the same name tells that origin story differently, with fresh targets and new circumstances.

Bond does not start out as a double-0 officer. Casino Royale treats the prefix as a status that must be earned, and the novel names two specific kills as the qualification.

The first kill takes place in Upcoming York. Bond's target there is a Japanese cipher expert, a specialist in codes.

In a recent development, the second takes place in Stockholm, the Swedish capital. That target is a Norwegian double agent, someone who appears to serve one side while secretly working for another.

It has been revealed that the two kills span two countries, the U.S. and Sweden. Both targets come from the intelligence trade itself. One deals in codes, and the other in divided loyalty. Neither is a soldier or a common criminal. Bond's qualifying work is aimed at the people who make up the spy business.

The 2006 film, starring Daniel Craig, reworks this backstory. It shows Bond's promotion in a black-and-white opening sequence. The monochrome sets those scenes apart from the color footage that follows. It marks them as the step that comes before the rest of the story.

Recent findings suggest that the sequence shows Bond killing two men. One is Dryden, a section chief, whom Bond confronts in Prague. The other is Fisher, Dryden's contact. Both men belong to the spy world, as the novel's targets do. These two deaths replace the novel's kills and earn the screen Bond his double-0 number.

Industry observers note that the film keeps the novel's count of two kills but changes the people involved. In the book, the targets are a cipher expert and a double agent. In the film, they are a section chief and his contact. The shape of the origin survives the adaptation, while its details belong to each version alone.

In a recent development, james Bond is not the only officer with a double-0 number in the Eon Productions films. Three others appear on screen: 006 in GoldenEye (1995), 009 in Octopussy (1983) and 004 in The Living Daylights (1987).

Industry observers note that all three carry the same double zero as Bond. Only the last digit changes from one officer to the next. That detail shows that 007 is one numbered post among several. It is not a label reserved for one man.

The 006 designation belongs to Alec Trevelyan. Sean Bean plays him in GoldenEye. Here the number comes with a full character name and a named actor. That ties the 006 post to a specific person in the story rather than leaving it as a digit.

According to recent reports, agent 009 appears in the opening of Octopussy. He is already dead when the audience first sees him. He is also disguised as a clown.

Agent 004 appears in the opening of The Living Daylights. He is killed during a training exercise.

Industry observers note that the two films use these officers in a similar way. In each, the other double-0 agent appears in the opening sequence rather than later in the story. Neither survives that sequence. The audience meets him only briefly, and his number matters more than his character.

Sources indicate that taken together, the three films sketch the double-0 section as a working unit with several members. On screen, Bond is one numbered officer within that group, and his place in it is 007.

In a recent development, in No Time to Die, the 2021 Bond film, the 007 designation belongs to someone other than James Bond. Bond has left the service, and an officer named Nomi, played by Lashana Lynch, carries the number.

Recent findings suggest that the story turns on that change in Bond's status. He is no longer working for MI6, the Secret Intelligence Service, when the events of the film take place. His exit leaves the code number open, and another officer holds it.

The detail demonstrates how the number works inside the fiction. The 007 code is tied to a post in the double-0 section, not to one particular man. When an officer leaves, the post remains, and so does its number.

According to recent reports, the film links two characters to the same three digits. Bond is the character audiences have connected with the number since Ian Fleming's novels. Nomi is the officer who holds it while the film's events unfold.

That arrangement treats 007 as a working designation that MI6 assigns. It is not a personal name that retires when one officer walks away.

According to recent reports, the license to kill is not real. MI6 has no double-0 section, and none of its officers holds a standing license to kill. Both exist only in Ian Fleming's novels and the films adapted from them.

In a recent development, MI6 is the Secret Intelligence Service. In the stories, it employs James Bond under the number 007. In reality, it has no numbered section of officers authorized to kill.

The closest real-world comparison is a piece of legislation, not a code number. Section 7 of the U.K. Intelligence Services Act 1994 lets the Secretary of State authorize certain acts outside the British Isles. These are acts that would otherwise break U.K. law.

Sources indicate that the purpose of that authorization is protection at home. Staff who carry out an authorized act abroad are shielded from liability in the U.K. for that act.

Industry observers note that section 7 is sometimes nicknamed the "James Bond clause." The nickname borrows from the fiction. It does not describe what the law permits.

Industry observers note that section 7 is not a license to kill. It gives no officer a personal, standing authority to take a life. The power to authorize sits with the Secretary of State, not with any individual officer.

Sources indicate that the difference from the fiction lies in where the authority comes from. In Fleming's stories, the double-0 prefix itself marks an officer authorized to kill in the line of duty. The authority travels with the officer's number.

Industry observers note that under the 1994 act, nothing travels with a number. The provision addresses whether staff face liability under U.K. law for an authorized act abroad. It does not create a class of officers set apart for lethal work.

In a recent development, for readers asking whether the license to kill is real, the answer has two parts. The double-0 license is an invention of the stories. The nearest real law works as a legal shield, not a grant of lethal power.

It has been revealed that ian Fleming, the novelist who created James Bond, worked in British naval intelligence during World War II. The phrase most closely tied to Bond's double-0 status later became the title of a 1989 Bond film, Licence to Kill.

Fleming's wartime post was real intelligence work. His spy fiction came afterward. Bond did not appear in print until several years after the war ended.

In a recent development, the order of events separates fact from invention. Fleming's naval service is part of the historical record. The double-0 section he later wrote about is not. Its authority to kill exists only in the novels and the films adapted from them.

It has been revealed that the name of his hero came from a different field altogether. Fleming borrowed the name James Bond from an American ornithologist. That James Bond wrote a field guide to the birds of the Caribbean. The fictional spy and the real bird expert share a name and nothing else.

Sources indicate that fleming wrote the Bond novels at Goldeneye, his home in Jamaica. The house shares its name with the 1995 Bond film GoldenEye. The film's title capitalizes the second E. The Caribbean runs through both details. The ornithologist's field guide covered the region's birds, and the novels were written on one of its islands.

Industry observers note that licence to Kill starred Timothy Dalton as Bond. It was the 16th Bond film made by Eon Productions, the production company behind the main Bond film series.

It has been revealed that the title keeps the British spelling, licence. In U.S. English, the same word is spelled license. Both spellings refer to the same authority attached to the double-0 prefix.

It has been revealed that the story turns the phrase around. In Licence to Kill, Bond acts without official sanction. The title names an authority the service grants, and the plot follows Bond working outside it. A film named for the license reveals its hero without the official backing that gives the double-0 number its meaning in the stories.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”.

Microsoft indicates active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft hasn’t noted what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate matter,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

It has been revealed that the gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the tech giant put it, so email stayed down.

In a recent development, microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t swiftly undo one that was months old.

The tech giant’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

According to recent reports, microsoft states it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put latest limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate matter,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

His advice to anyone starting out is to share the load.

Binance has published the final results of an unscheduled Proof of Reserves (PoR) report, two weeks after the cryptocurrency exchange lost $6.34 billion in an October hack.

In a recent development, according to Binance, the snapshot was taken on Nov. 12 at 00:00 UTC, and it shows that the exchange fully backs the balances of its clients. Shiba Inu (SHIB) is backed at 100.04%, and the other major assets on the exchange are fully covered as well.

Industry observers note that the latest report comes after the Oct. 29 attack, during which hackers stole funds from Binance across ten blockchains in 20 minutes. Among the stolen funds were nearly 500 billion SHIB. After the attack, the exchange took an additional reserve snapshot at Bitcoin block height 975493.

Recent findings suggest that binance data shows that the net account balances of customers stand at 50.67 trillion SHIB, and the exchange holds 50.69 trillion SHIB in its wallets. Of that amount, 50.68 trillion SHIB is held at the addresses of Binance itself, and the remaining 7.46 billion SHIB is held by third-party custodians.

Besides SHIB, the report also reveals that the other major cryptocurrencies are fully backed. Compared with the previous check on Nov. 4, the BTC balances of customers went up by 0.35% to 687,912 BTC, and the coverage ratio for Bitcoin stands at 100.05%. The ETH balances went up by 1.04% to 3.48 million ETH, and the BNB balances increased by 1.03% to 42.95 million BNB.

Still, the USDT balances of people went down by 3.68% to 24.3 billion USDT. At the same time, the stablecoin has the highest coverage ratio in the report at 104.34%.

Arkham Intelligence data shows that the known wallets of Binance right now hold 58.82 trillion SHIB. That is 5.88% of the total supply of the meme coin, and these tokens are worth $251.16 million. In this context, Binance wallets hold 8.13 trillion SHIB (about $34.7 million) more than the amount shown in the PoR report.

According to Binance, the PoR report only covers the deposits of clients and the coins that the exchange keeps to back them, so the company's own funds are not included in the report. Based on the Arkham data, Binance holds about 16% more SHIB than it owes to its clients.

According to Arkham, Binance is still the third-largest exchange by SHIB holdings. Only the burn address with 410.44 trillion SHIB (or 41.04% of supply), the U.S.-based exchange Coinbase with 74.53 trillion SHIB, and South Korea's Upbit with 64.14 trillion SHIB hold more of the meme coin. Robinhood, Crypto.com and Bithumb come after Binance with 57.12 trillion, 34.95 trillion and 16.74 trillion SHIB, respectively.

At press time, the price of SHIB stands at $0.00000426.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Who owns James Bond? Rights to 007 are split among Ian Fleming's estate, Danjaq and Amazon MGM Studios, shaped by decades of deals and legal disputes.

According to recent reports, james Bond is one character with several owners. The books that introduced him belong to one organization. The films are controlled by others. For years, a third party also held a claim to some of his best-known enemies. Anyone asking who owns James Bond is really asking about a set of separate rights. Those rights have been bought, sold, contested and divided many times.

The story begins with Ian Fleming, the British author who created Bond on the page. His literary rights sit with Ian Fleming Publications. The screen rights followed a different path. In the 1960s, producers Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman set up Danjaq as a holding tech giant to control the film franchise. A related company, Eon Productions, makes the movies.

Industry observers note that that arrangement did not stay fixed. Saltzman sold his stake to United Artists in 1975. The sale turned a Hollywood studio into a partner in the film rights. The studio's share later sat with MGM, which also distributes the films in the U.S.

A separate fight ran alongside the main franchise. Filmmaker Kevin McClory spent years in a legal battle over the story behind Thunderball. He won rights tied to its story elements, including the criminal organization SPECTRE and its leader, Ernst Stavro Blofeld. Those rights made room for a Bond film outside the official series, Never Say Never Again, released in 1983. MGM and Danjaq later acquired the McClory interests and ended the dispute.

Amazon $AMZN is the newest name in that chain. The tech giant announced a deal to buy MGM in May 2021 and completed it in March 2022. With MGM came the studio's stake in the films. In February 2025, Amazon MGM Studios reached an agreement with Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, the longtime Eon producers. Under it, Amazon took creative control of the franchise. Broccoli and Wilson remain co-owners of the Bond intellectual property through Danjaq.

Recent findings suggest that the 10 slides that follow take these ownership events one at a time. They cover the author, the companies, the studio sales, the legal battle and the most recent deal. Each explains who holds which piece of 007, how it changed hands and who now shapes the character's future on screen. They are a selection of the main moments, not a complete legal history of the franchise.

Recent findings suggest that james Bond began as a character in a book, not a film. British author Ian Fleming introduced him in Casino Royale, a spy novel published in the U.K. in 1953. Every later claim to the 007 rights traces back to that novel and the books that followed it.

Fleming wrote the manuscript in early 1952 at Goldeneye, his house on the north coast of Jamaica. The London publisher Jonathan Cape released it in April 1953. Bond arrived as an established agent, with the 007 designation already assigned to him.

It has been revealed that the plot is compact. Britain's Secret Service sends Bond to a casino in Royale-les-Eaux, a fictional resort town in northern France. His target is Le Chiffre, an agent working for the Soviet Union who has lost money he cannot account for. Bond's task is to beat him at baccarat and leave him ruined.

According to recent reports, fleming drew on his own career for the setting. During World War II, he served in British naval intelligence. He worked as personal assistant to Admiral John Godfrey, the director of naval intelligence. That experience gave the book its attention to tradecraft, office politics and the mechanics of espionage.

In a recent development, the character's name has its own origin. Fleming borrowed it from James Bond, an American ornithologist who wrote a field guide to the birds of the West Indies. Fleming wanted a name that sounded plain, and the bird expert's name suited that purpose.

In a recent development, casino Royale was the first of 12 Bond novels. Fleming also wrote Bond short stories, collected in For Your Eyes Only in 1960 and in Octopussy and The Living Daylights, published after his death. Fleming died in 1964. His final novel, The Man with the Golden Gun, appeared the following year.

In a recent development, the novels supplied the characters, titles and plots that producers later adapted for the screen. Film titles such as Dr. No, Goldfinger and Thunderball come directly from Fleming's books. That literary source is the starting point for every rights question that followed, from the books themselves to the films and the disputes over them.

Sources indicate that the rights to Ian Fleming's James Bond novels belong to Ian Fleming Publications, the organization that represents the author's estate. The company was previously known as Glidrose.

According to recent reports, both names refer to the same rights holder. Glidrose is the older name. Ian Fleming Publications is the name the organization uses today.

This ownership covers Bond on the page. Fleming's novels are the original source of the character, and the literary rights attach to those books.

It has been revealed that the films are a separate matter. The movie series has its own chain of owners. Danjaq LLC holds the film franchise, and Eon Productions makes the films.

That split is why the question of who owns James Bond has more than one answer. A question about the novels points to Ian Fleming Publications. A question about the movies points to Danjaq, Eon and the studio partners that have held a share of the film rights over the decades.

Industry observers note that the two sides of Bond have also followed different histories. The film rights have passed through several hands. The literary rights have stayed with the manufacturer tied to Fleming's estate, under its old name and its current one.

Studio deals involving MGM concern the film franchise. On their own terms, they are not transactions over Fleming's books.

Industry observers note that danjaq LLC is the holding manufacturer behind the James Bond film franchise. Producers Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman set it up in the 1960s to hold their rights to the 007 movies.

Broccoli, known as Cubby, was an American producer who wanted to bring the books to the screen. Saltzman, who was born in Canada, had secured an option on most of Fleming's novels before the two men teamed up. Their partnership paired Broccoli's interest in the books with Saltzman's option.

The company's name comes from its founders' wives. It joins the first names of Dana Broccoli and Jacqueline Saltzman.

Danjaq's role is ownership rather than filmmaking. It holds the franchise's rights. Eon Productions, a separate tech giant, handles the production of each film.

It has been revealed that that split matters for anyone tracing who controls Bond on screen. The character began in Ian Fleming's novels, and the books remain a separate property. Danjaq's interest covers the film franchise, not Fleming's writing.

Recent findings suggest that united Artists was tied to the franchise from the start. The studio financed and distributed Dr. No, the first Eon Bond film, in 1962.

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

According to recent reports, amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Industry observers note that over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The Latest York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

According to recent reports, pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk.

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson noted. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”.

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”.

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”.

According to recent reports, fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others remarked the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

Sources indicate that I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

In a recent development, “No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”.

The idea answers a practical question that faces any long-running film series. The Eon Productions films have recast their lead several times, from Sean Connery to Daniel Craig. The series rarely explains a recasting on screen. A new face appears in the tuxedo, and the story moves on.

Time is the other problem the theory tries to solve. Read as one unbroken career, the films would follow a single field agent across several decades of missions. A rotating name removes that strain.

The setting points the same way. A casino table is a social space, not an MI6 briefing room. Bond gives his name there as any guest at the table might, rather than reciting an official designation.

The scene matters for the code-name theory. Any case that "James Bond" is a cover identity has to account for the character's first screen introduction. In Dr. No, the name arrives as a personal introduction from the man himself.

Ian Fleming created James Bond in Casino Royale, published in 1953, and wrote him as one specific man. Nothing in Fleming's novels presents the name as a title passed from agent to agent.

According to recent reports, fleming was a British journalist who had served in naval intelligence. During World War II, he worked as an assistant to the U.K.'s Director of Naval Intelligence. That background informs the codes, briefings and field operations in his books.

The name has a documented origin. Fleming borrowed it from James Bond, an American ornithologist who wrote Birds of the West Indies. Fleming wanted a plain, unremarkable name for his hero. He took it from a real person rather than inventing a cover identity.

Casino Royale sends Bond to a French resort on an MI6 assignment. His target is Le Chiffre, a Soviet-linked operative who has lost money he does not control. Bond's job is to beat him at baccarat and leave him unable to cover the losses.

The novel also explains how Bond got his 00 prefix. He tells an ally that he earned it by killing two people on assignment. One was a Japanese cipher expert in New York. The other was a Norwegian double agent in Stockholm. In Fleming's telling, the number reflects a record of specific acts by one agent.

Fleming kept writing the same character across 12 novels and two short story collections. Some of that work appeared after his death in 1964. Characters such as M and the CIA's Felix Leiter recur, and later books refer back to earlier missions.

The most detailed biography arrives in You Only Live Twice, published in 1964. After Bond is presumed dead, M writes an obituary of him for The Times. It sets out his parents, childhood, schooling and naval career. That record describes a single person with a single life story.

The code-name theory concerns the films, where a series of actors stepped into the role. Readers of the books meet one James Bond, written by one author over roughly a decade. Any case for a shared code name has to rest on what the movies added, not on Fleming's source material.

In the opening of On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969), George Lazenby's Bond turns to the camera and notes, "This never happened to the other fellow." Fans cite the line as support for the theory that James Bond is a code name.

According to recent reports, lazenby followed Sean Connery, who had played Bond since the series began. That made Lazenby the first actor to take over a role audiences knew from only one face. Placing the line in the opening means the film addresses the recasting almost as soon as Lazenby appears.

Bond speaks the line to the camera, not to another character. That makes it a direct aside to the audience. For a moment, Bond steps outside the story and acknowledges the people watching it.

Industry observers note that one reading treats "the other fellow" as a reference to Connery. On that view, the joke concerns the casting change, not anything that happens inside MI6. The film signals that it knows a new actor is playing a familiar character.

Code-name theorists read the same words another way. If "James Bond" were a title passed between MI6 agents, the other fellow could be an earlier agent who held it. The line would then be an in-story remark about a predecessor, not a joke about an actor.

The words alone do not decide between those readings. The line names no one. It claims nothing about MI6 assigning names, and it does not mention a 00 number or a handover.

It has been revealed that the rest of the film complicates the code-name reading. On Her Majesty's Secret Service is the film in which Bond marries Tracy. A later film returns to that marriage as part of Bond's own past, with a different actor in the role.

In a recent development, the producers at Eon Productions have not confirmed the code-name theory as official continuity. That leaves the line open to both readings, with no official answer attached.

Sources indicate that for Your Eyes Only (1981) demonstrates Roger Moore's Bond at the grave of his wife, Tracy. Bond married Tracy in On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969), a film that starred George Lazenby. The scene presents two actors as one man with a single shared past.

That detail bears directly on the code-name theory. Under that theory, "James Bond" would be a title passed from one MI6 agent to the next. A new agent who inherited the name would have no personal reason to visit another man's wife.

To absorb the scene, the theory would have to treat the successor as a man who took on his predecessor's grief along with his name. Nothing in the scene suggests that. Moore's Bond visits the grave as a widower, not as a colleague paying respects.

Industry observers note that the grave scene only works if Moore's Bond is the same person who married Tracy. The film asks the audience to accept that his history carries over. A different actor lived through that history on screen.

Moore's first outing as Bond came in Live and Let Die (1973), four years after On Her Majesty's Secret Service was released. He reached the scene at Tracy's grave eight years after that debut.

It has been revealed that the wedding film and the graveside film sit 12 years apart. Across that span, the actor playing Bond changed. The character's widowhood did not.

That gap highlights how the series treats its own record. The marriage belongs to the character, not to the actor who performed it. A recast did not erase it.

Sources indicate that the scene gives the series a direct continuity link between actors. It ties a later Bond to an event from Lazenby's film. It does not, however, give an in-story reason for why Bond looks different.

Sources indicate that that leaves viewers with a fixed point rather than a full answer. The face changed between 1969 and 1981. The marriage, and the loss behind it, stayed attached to the same man.

M and Q return throughout the Bond films, but the actors who play them change over time. Supporters of the code-name theory treat that turnover as a sign the series handles key roles as posts that different people can fill.

M is the head of Bond's service and the figure who sends him on his assignments. Q runs the department that supplies his equipment. On screen, both characters are known by a single letter rather than a full name. A letter reads more like a job title than like a person's identity, and that is the detail the theory leans on.

Recent findings suggest that judi Dench played M from GoldenEye (1995) through Skyfall (2012). Her run covers 17 years. It also straddles Casino Royale (2006), the film that restarted the series with a new origin story for Bond. The same actor therefore held the role of M on both sides of that reset. The character stayed in place even as the series began Bond's story again.

Sources indicate that skyfall also highlights the M title changing hands inside the story itself. Dench's M dies in that film. Gareth Mallory, played by Ralph Fiennes, then takes over the post. Here the films treat M openly as an office that one person leaves and another fills.

The code-name theory builds on this kind of continuity. If a letter-based title can move from one actor to the next, the argument goes, the name James Bond might work the same way. On that reading, each fresh Bond actor would be playing a new agent who inherits the name along with the job.

The comparison has a limit. M and Q are presented as designations tied to a position inside the service. James Bond is presented as a personal name, the one he gives when he introduces himself. Mallory keeps his own name when he becomes M. A new face behind a single-letter title indicates that the office can change hands. It does not show that a man's own name can.

The M and Q pattern is consistent with the code-name theory, but it does not establish it.

It has been revealed that casino Royale (2006) restarted the James Bond film series with Daniel Craig in the lead. The film demonstrates Bond earning his 00 status, telling his origin as a upcoming story rather than continuing an old one.

According to recent reports, that structure matters for the code-name theory. A code name implies a line of agents. Each would take the identity from the agent who held it before him. The newest holder would arrive with a predecessor's history already attached.

A reboot works differently. It sets the earlier films aside and starts the same character's life again from an earlier point. Nothing is inherited. The earlier adventures no longer form part of his record.

It has been revealed that craig's Bond is not presented as a recruit stepping into an established identity. He is James Bond at the start of his career, before he holds a license to kill. His promotion to 00 status is the event the story builds from.

That sequence runs against the code-name reading. Under the theory, the name would come with the 007 post. In Casino Royale, the order is reversed. The man already has the name, and he has to earn the number. The promotion confers the 00 prefix, not the identity.

The film's title also signals a fresh start. Casino Royale shares its name with Ian Fleming's first Bond novel. By borrowing that title, the 2006 film returns to the character's starting point instead of picking up from the most recent adventure.

According to recent reports, the reboot leaves one loose thread. Judi Dench, who first played M in GoldenEye (1995), stays in the role for Casino Royale. The same actor in the same part sits on both sides of the restart.

Sources indicate that the film does not explain that overlap. It also does not present Craig's Bond as the agent from the earlier films. The casting carries over, while the story begins again.

Industry observers note that skyfall (2012) takes Bond to his family estate in Scotland and establishes that his parents are dead. Those two details give the name James Bond a personal history. A code name passed between agents would carry no such history.

Sources indicate that the estate shares its name with the film. Skyfall is not an MI6 safe house or a cover identity. It is the Bond family's property, and the film presents it as the place Bond comes from.

That detail cuts against the code-name theory. The theory holds that "James Bond" is a title handed from one agent to the next. A title does not come with a family home. It does not come with a mother and a father either.

It has been revealed that skyfall attaches both to the name. The man called James Bond in this film is the son of a specific family. The house in Scotland belongs to that family. For the theory to hold, that history would have to belong to someone other than the agent using the name. The film gives no sign of a split like that.

It has been revealed that the family link also changes what the surname means. If the estate belongs to the Bond family, then "Bond" came to him through his parents, not through an MI6 posting. In this film the name is inherited at birth rather than issued with a job.

The film's title points in the same direction. Rather than naming a villain, a weapon or a mission, Skyfall takes its name from a private house. That choice ties the title to Bond's own past rather than to his work.

Recent findings suggest that the film belongs to the Daniel Craig run of the series, which began with a fresh origin story. Where that story showed his promotion to 00 status, Skyfall reaches further back, to the family behind the agent.

It has been revealed that the evidence has limits. Skyfall describes the Craig-era Bond only. It does not connect its family history to the versions played by earlier actors. On its own terms, the film shows that within one continuity, James Bond is a real name with a family behind it.

In the Bond films, the 00 prefix marks an agent with a license to kill. Bond is not the only agent who holds one, so the number works as a post within MI6 rather than a personal name.

In a recent development, goldenEye (1995) highlights this through 006, an agent played by Sean Bean. He and Bond are both 00 agents in the same service. Their numbers sit one apart. The designation is a slot that MI6 fills, and the film gives it to a different man with a different face.

It has been revealed that octopussy (1983) does the same with 009. His appearance indicates that the series put other licensed agents on screen 12 years before GoldenEye. Across the two films, the 00 roster includes men besides Bond, and each holds his own number.

Recent findings suggest that that pattern bears directly on the code name debate. A number that several agents can hold works the way fans imagine the name James Bond works. The films treat 007 as a designation an agent is assigned. They treat James Bond as the man who holds it.

Industry observers note that casino Royale (2006) adds a related detail. The film shows Bond earning his 00 status. He is already in MI6's service when the number arrives. He has the name before he has the number. The number is something MI6 grants. The name is something he already carries.

The name follows a different pattern from the number. Within each version of the series, the character called James Bond is one person. He carries his own history and his own relationships. The 00 prefix describes what he is licensed to do. The name describes who he is.

Industry observers note that this separates two ideas the code name theory tends to merge. The films do contain a handed-down role, and it is the number. A viewer looking for something passed between agents can find it in the 00 designations themselves, which more than one officer can hold. The name James Bond stays attached to one man in each version.

In a recent development, eon Productions, the firm run by Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, has never formally declared a single continuity for the James Bond films. No official statement confirms that "James Bond" is a code name. None lays out a timeline that links every film.

It has been revealed that that leaves the films as the record. Eon has produced the series since Dr. No in 1962. What appears on screen is the main guide to how Bond's history fits together.

On screen, the evidence points in two directions. Some films carry one man's past across different actors. Others restart the story with a latest origin.

It has been revealed that the cross-actor links rest on specific scenes. For Your Eyes Only (1981) shows Roger Moore's Bond at the grave of Tracy. Bond married her in On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969), when George Lazenby held the role. The scene treats both actors as the same person with a shared past.

Casino Royale (2006) breaks that chain. Daniel Craig's Bond earns his 00 status in that film. His career starts over rather than continuing from earlier entries.

The reboot did not replace everyone. Judi Dench played M from GoldenEye (1995) through Skyfall (2012). That span means the same actor held the role on both sides of the 2006 restart. A recurring character can carry over even when Bond's own story begins again.

According to recent reports, skyfall (2012) then gives the Craig version a family estate in Scotland and parents who have died. Those details tie the name to an individual with a birth family, not to a title handed between agents.

Industry observers note that the 00 number works differently. Other agents in the films hold numbers such as 006 and 009. That pattern marks the number as an assignment. The name stays attached to one man in each version.

Sources indicate that without a formal statement from the producers, the code-name idea remains a fan theory. What the films show is one man's story running across several actors, followed by a reboot that started it again.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that one of Ethereum's consensus clients has merged a fix for a validator pubkey cache poisoning attack, according to a pull request on GitHub.
  • Gloas is the consensus layer part of the upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade.
  • The issue lies in a mechanism where the client stores validator public keys and their indexes in a global cache.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that one of Ethereum's consensus clients has merged a fix for a validator pubkey cache poisoning attack, according to a pull request on GitHub. The patch addresses a vulnerability around the Gloas fork, which could result in some nodes rejecting valid signatures due to a bug in the global pubkey cache.

Gloas is the consensus layer part of the upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade.

The issue lies in a mechanism where the client stores validator public keys and their indexes in a global cache.

Technically, deposits that are already finalized should give the same validators on every chain, though it is a different story at the fork boundary.

The attacker needs 3 pending deposits just before the fork. The first one is a large top-up for an existing validator. The other two are fresh keys: A with builder credentials and B with regular validator credentials.

On the canonical chain, the top-up consumes the balance churn, so A and B are processed after the fork. A becomes a builder, and B takes the next validator index.

It has been revealed that on the attacker's side chain, the topped-up validator gets slashed before the fork, and its deposit is skipped. This leads to A being processed earlier, essentially taking B's index.

The buggy cache assumed both chains would produce the same validators and imported A's key globally.

At the fork, affected nodes would reject all valid signatures from B on the canonical chain and fork off.

Realistically, the attack is somewhat complicated, as it needs a slashing at the right moment and a side chain, so it's unlikely to happen by accident.

According to the PR, the fix is to only add keys to the global pubkey cache once their activation eligibility epoch is finalized.

A upcoming HeadPubkeys structure also combines keys from the head state and the global cache, so nodes don't miss keys if the chain finalizes without new blocks.

Recent findings suggest that whether other consensus clients had a similar problem is yet to be confirmed. In other words, the closer Glamsterdam gets, the more edge cases around the fork boundary developers have to catch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication.
  • Sources indicate that the FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication.
  • It has been revealed that again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

Sources indicate that the FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

It has been revealed that again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

In a recent development, the FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

According to recent reports, the agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”.

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he claims. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs.".

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

According to recent reports, so…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's vital to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali indicates. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications.".

It has been revealed that dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he indicates. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions.".

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh notes. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.

She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delta CEO Ed Bastian notes one of his airline’s oldest routes is slower now than when it launched in the 1950s, and it’s “absurd.”.

“Today, it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first released that flight, which is absurd,” Bastian told Fortune’s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on Monday.

His complaint lands days after the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide grounding of flights last week put the country’s congested air traffic control system back in the spotlight. Bastian said fixing it would bring ticket prices down by letting airlines add flights, but modernization can’t happen without investment, which doesn’t seem likely when the data-center buildout is diverting trillions in capital.

“We can’t even get $50 billion to fix our skies, which affects all of us at a much higher level than any individual data center,” Bastian said.

Airplanes have become more advanced since the one equipped for the world’s first scheduled commercial flight from St. Petersburg to Tampa over a century ago. By Bastian’s account, the system they fly through hasn’t kept up.

Delta is also grappling with airfare pricing after the Iran war’s pressure on jet fuel prices squeezed the airline industry, and it has passed much of that cost onto consumers. Bastian said Delta’s tickets are 15% to 20% higher year-over-year because of jet fuel, adding that this wouldn’t have been possible to do if there wasn’t sufficient demand.

“We would not be able to generate that type of pricing if we didn’t have a consumer that was willing to pay it, and so that tells you the core demand is really healthy, even if pricing is where it’s at,” Bastian said.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ October release, U.S. airfares climbed 22.4% year over year as airlines raised prices to offset the higher cost of jet fuel. That helped the five major airlines generate $8.8 billion more in Q3 2026 than in Q3 2025, but passenger traffic grew less than 1%. Bastian said that instead of competing on fares with other airlines, Delta is trying to draw more passengers by distinguishing itself from its competition through service.

“If you don’t have people that are there to serve our customers in a premium manner, the rest of the stuff doesn’t really matter, and that’s the one thing that our competitors cannot replicate,” he said.

He said 15 years of cultivating that premium customer service culture came through during the FAA flight shutdown. While he said he typically hears compliments about the service on most weekends, this one was special because of the disruption coming from outside of Delta’s control.

“Unlike most weekends, when there’s always something going wrong or excuses somewhere, the overwhelming sentiment I received from customers was, ‘You have amazing people’ because they saw the stress, the conditions [were] none of our doing,” he stated.

That’s also why Bastian said AI won’t replace Delta employees. Instead, the tech giant will redeploy affected employees to the extent possible because “there’s always something to do.” He said this is because when there’s a crisis like the FAA one, customers prefer human support over machines.

“Obviously this past weekend, they wanted individuals to tell them what was going on, and there’s a lack of trust the more you put technology in place of humans, so humans are always going to be at the center of Delta,” he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:16 am.
  • A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S.
  • The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:16 am.

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

In a recent development, “What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, noted in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”.

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

It has been revealed that in the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for newly introduced and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

In a recent development, nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

Sources indicate that all three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for upcoming clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the manufacturer to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst mentioned in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”.

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that every founder knows this call. The demo went perfectly, the person who would use your product is thrilled and she promises to push it through. Then the deal goes quiet for three months. Founders blame inertia or a weak champion.

More often, the person who loved the product was never the person who could buy it, and nobody had mapped the people who could.

This is the limit of standard startup advice: find the user in pain, win their advocacy.

Recent findings suggest that and let them pull the product inside. That bottom-up motion works where consumers control the budget. It fails wherever a purchase has to clear finance, IT, legal and operations. I learned this early in my career selling orthopedic medical devices, where a surgeon could love an implant and the hospital still would not buy it. Since then, I have watched the same mistake stall more good products, in more industries, than competitors ever did.

In Strategic Selling, Robert Miller and Stephen Heiman describe four roles that show up in a complex B2B sale:.

Most startups spend their time with the User Buyer and assume she’s also their Coach. The way to tell is access. A Coach gets you in front of the CFO, tells you when procurement reviews the contract and warns you about last quarter’s objection from finance. Someone who loves your product but won’t do those things is a fan, and fans don’t close deals.

According to recent reports, the room is bigger than most founders assume. A Gartner survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in May 2025, found buying groups ranging from five to 16 people across as many as four functions and 74% of those groups showed unhealthy conflict: members with conflicting objectives, disagreement on the best course, or decisions overruled by outsiders. Forrester’s 2026 research puts the typical buying decision at 13 internal stakeholders and nine external influencers.

Healthcare is an extreme case, not an exception. In a 2025 HIMSS survey of 211 health IT buyers, 57% noted five or more people take part in technology purchases, and 23% said ten or more. Hospitals add value analysis committees on top. IQVIA reported in 2023, based on a survey of committee members, that even after approval only about one third of products are cleared for broad use. The rest must prove themselves in a trial, and Forrester found that more than 60% of business buyers across industries now use a trial before they buy.

It has been revealed that the Challenger Sale by Matthew Dixon and Brent Adamson is the best playbook I know for this. Across more than 6,000 reps, those who challenged customer thinking made up nearly 40% of star performers and 54% in complex sales. Relationship builders made up 7%. Being liked won’t get you through a committee.

Industry observers note that almost nobody does this work. Our 2026 State of B2B Go-to-Market report, which surveyed 511 B2B professionals, found that roughly 24% of go-to-market spending goes to initiatives with no traceable commercial outcome. That gap is the opportunity. A team with a documented buyer map can walk each decision gate on purpose while competitors wonder why the deal went cold. Here is how I start:.

According to recent reports, selling medical devices taught me that the market isn’t irrational. The map most teams carry into it is incomplete. You can keep building for the person who loves your product and wonder why the deal stalls in a room you never entered, or you can find out who holds the budget and what they are measured on. Most teams don’t have a pipeline problem. They have a buyer map problem.

Every founder knows this call. The demo went perfectly, the person who would use your product is thrilled and she promises to push it through. Then the deal goes quiet for three months. Founders blame inertia or a weak champion.

More often, the person who loved the product was never the person who could buy it, and nobody had mapped the people who could.

This is the limit of standard startup advice: find the user in pain, win their advocacy.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that ioffe’s company uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data, and recommend solutions to business problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI is already fueling workers’ fears of being replaced. Now, one startup CEO predicts it could soon help companies decide whether to lay them off, too.

“We do expect that within the next few years, the majority of significant enterprise shifts, whether it’s products you’re launching, you know, layoffs that you’re making, et cetera, will be recommended by agents,” Michael Ioffe, cofounder and CEO of Arist, noted while speaking with Fortune‘s Kristin Stoller at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Industry observers note that ioffe’s company uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data, and recommend solutions to business problems. Arist already works with more than 15% of the Fortune 500, and its technology can gather insights from thousands of employees in just 72 hours—a process that traditionally requires teams of consultants. Still, he doesn’t envision executives handing over control entirely.

“At the end of the day, it will always be an executive who is making the final call,” Ioffe said.

Recent findings suggest that that prediction comes as more companies cite AI when cutting jobs, sometimes drawing accusations of “AI washing,” or blaming technology for cuts made for other reasons. But even when companies genuinely expect AI to replace workers, moving too quickly can backfire. As Stoller previously reported, HR leaders have warned that companies risk losing valuable talent when they cut workers without a clear strategy for how AI will replace their work.

For Ioffe, the appeal is speed. When sales fall or a product struggles, companies often spend months and millions of dollars working with consultants to understand why. He believes AI can help executives get answers in days rather than months.

It has been revealed that ioffe didn’t set out to compete with consulting firms. At 19, he became interested in delivering education to students in war-torn Yemen and built a text-message-based learning platform, then shifted Arist toward training employees at Fortune 500 companies, becoming one of OpenAI’s early partners along the way.

He started to notice a pattern: companies would pay consultants millions to diagnose a problem, then pay Arist a few hundred thousand dollars to train employees to fix it. In his experience, the consultants got the diagnosis wrong about 90% of the time.

That prompted Arist to move from training employees to diagnosing the problems companies were trying to solve. Ioffe pointed to a major software firm whose data was merely pointing out what was happening instead of why.

Before AI can recommend something as consequential as a layoff, it first needs to understand what’s happening inside a company. Arist’s agents can decide whom to interview, ask questions, and weigh responses against information such as an employee’s tenure, performance, and past engagement scores. Ioffe remarked that helps the system distinguish the loudest complaints from problems affecting the wider organization. The agents will also push back, he said, if an executive frames a question to get the answer they want.

But gathering that information could raise concerns about how candid employees are willing to be with an AI agent working on behalf of their employer, especially when its findings could influence decisions about their jobs.

Ioffe argued that employees may actually be more candid with AI agents than with another person, making it easier for companies to uncover problems that might otherwise go unreported.

“Turns out that humans are not that good at listening,” he quipped.

Rather than replacing executives or consultants, Ioffe sees AI’s biggest opportunity in helping companies identify problems and act on them faster.

“If you can get to the truth much faster, then a 50,000-person enterprise can move at the speed of a 50-person startup,” Ioffe noted.

The first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011, by David Schwartz.

According to the official XRP account on X, the date 11/11/11 marked the beginning of Schwartz's work on what would later support one of the cryptocurrency industry's established payment-focused blockchain networks.

Recent findings suggest that schwartz, now Ripple CTO Emeritus, was one of three engineers, alongside Jed McCaleb and Arthur Britto, who began developing the XRP Ledger in 2011. The three were inspired by Bitcoin to build an alternative that would address some of its problems, especially in the areas of sustainability and payments.

In June 2012, the XRP Ledger went live. Shortly after Chris Larsen joined the group in September 2012, a firm called NewCoin was formed; it soon changed its name to OpenCoin before becoming Ripple. The founders of the XRPL donated 80 billion XRP, the network’s native digital asset, to the company.

Ripple has locked up most of its XRP in escrow, about 55 billion XRP, and releases 1 billion XRP on the first day of every month.

The anniversary on November 11 marks the start of the XRP Ledger’s development, as what began with Schwartz's first code in 2011 eventually morphed into a blockchain network designed to enable value transfers.

November is also a big month for XRP as U.S. spot XRP ETFs celebrate the first anniversary of their landmark launch.Canary Capital’s XRP exchange-traded fund, listed under the ticker XRPC, began trading on November 13, 2025, and is the first spot XRP ETF on a U.S. exchange.

According to recent reports, in upgrade news, XRPL version 3.5.0 is scheduled for December 3, 2026. This release includes only improvements and fixes, including a permanent fix for occasional slow ledger close times.

Sources indicate that you don’t need an advertising budget to find your first customers. You need a product people love, a way to tell whether they really love it, and the patience to let them spread the word.

It has been revealed that that’s the lesson from Katina Mountanos, founder and CEO of Kosterina, a wellness brand built around high-antioxidant extra virgin olive oil and the modern Mediterranean diet. She launched it as a passion project while working full-time at Walmart and found her first 50 to 100 customers without paid ads. When Kosterina had about 100 customers, a simple survey returned a perfect Net Promoter Score of 100, and Whole Foods found the brand on Instagram and reached out on its own.
