Sources indicate that kosterina’s earliest customers were almost exclusively friends and family. For many founders, that can feel like it doesn’t count. Mountanos sees it differently: the people closest to you are the fastest, cheapest way to get a product into real hands and start learning.

In a recent development, the key is what happens after that first order. Kosterina’s growth beyond its founder’s immediate circle came from repeat purchases and referrals, not from ads. Friends and family reordered, then passed the product along to people Mountanos didn’t know. That chain of recommendations became the brand’s first real marketing engine.

Every founder selling to friends and family faces the same question: do these people genuinely love the product, or are they just being supportive?

In a recent development, mountanos suggested looking past the first sale and watching what customers do next. Three behaviors matter most:.

Those signals, she noted, say far more about a business’s potential than a count of initial sales.

According to recent reports, when Kosterina reached roughly 100 customers, Mountanos sent out a Net Promoter Score survey. NPS asks one simple question: how likely are you to recommend this product to a friend? Scores range from -100 to 100.

Sources indicate that having used NPS across brands during her time at Walmart, Mountanos knew how rare that result was. She took it as a strong signal that customers didn’t just like the product; they were eager to recommend it. It was one of the moments that convinced her Kosterina could be more than a passion project.

In a recent development, for early-stage founders, the lesson is that validation doesn’t require expensive research. A free survey sent to your first 100 customers can show whether you have a foundation worth building on, and where you need to improve.

One of the most common mistakes Mountanos sees is founders holding a product back until every detail is right. She’s a believer in rapid prototyping: get something into the market, collect feedback, and use that loop to keep improving.

Sources indicate that launching early does two things at once. It gets you customers sooner, and it highlights you what those customers actually want, which is rarely exactly what you imagined. Each round of feedback makes the next version of the product, and the pitch behind it, stronger.

Without a budget to outspend competitors, Kosterina leaned on the things it could control: the product, the packaging and the story behind them.

Recent findings suggest that make the product worth sharing. Early on, the team stayed focused on high-quality EVOO and distinctive packaging. The goal was simple: give customers something they’d want to buy again, recommend and show off.

It has been revealed that get it into people’s hands. Mountanos views sampling as one of the most effective acquisition tools, because tasting the product can turn a skeptic into a loyal customer. Kosterina also treats gifting as a form of sampling. People who receive a bottle as a gift often become customers themselves.

Sources indicate that educate, don’t just advertise. Most shoppers don’t know much about olive oil quality, or why high-polyphenol EVOO is different. Kosterina filled that gap with content on EVOO, the Mediterranean diet, recipes and broader wellness. That gave people a reason to engage with the brand beyond a product ad, and it costs far less than paid media.

Industry observers note that build a brand people notice. Kosterina’s branding opened doors before the company had scale. Whole Foods discovered the brand on Instagram and reached out directly, and Mountanos has credited the packaging with putting Kosterina on the retailer’s radar. Putting something compelling into the world can create opportunities you’d never be able to buy.

Be ready to change the plan. Kosterina’s Whole Foods launch was built around in-store sampling. Then COVID hit, and the brand couldn’t sample in stores for more than a year. The team had to find other ways to reach new customers, a reminder that early-stage businesses need more than one path to the people they’re trying to reach.

In a recent development, mountanos didn’t quit her job to start Kosterina. She built the brand alongside her full-time role at Walmart, which gave her time to develop the product and gather real evidence of demand before committing to the business full time.

According to recent reports, that approach kept the risk low. Instead of betting her savings on an untested idea, she let customers prove it: repeat orders, referrals, a perfect NPS score and an inbound call from Whole Foods. Only then did the passion project become the main event.

According to recent reports, for founders working with limited resources, the same priorities apply. Put your money and time into the product itself and into getting it in front of people who can taste, use and talk about it. Be cautious about spending heavily on advertising, or on polishing every detail, before you’ve seen proof that customers will come back and bring others with them.

If you’ve been waiting for a budget before you get started, this conversation is worth your time. Mountanos indicates how a product people love, a few honest signals from early customers and some scrappy marketing took Kosterina from passion project to national retail.

In a recent development, stop waiting for the budget. Start with the customers you can reach today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Jensen Huang’s resignation has put a renewed spotlight on the U.S.-China race for dominance in chips and artificial intelligence, another technological contest could have even more direct national security implications: hypersonic weapons.

And the U.S. is already trailing behind, according to Andrew Kreitz, cofounder and CFO of Castelion—a $13 billion defense startup focused on developing hypersonic missiles.

“Unfortunately, China, especially, full stop, is ahead of us in hypersonics,” Kreitz told Fortune’s Andrew Nusca at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, Mich.

The U.S., for its part, has begun fielding its first long-range hypersonic missile system, known as “Dark Eagle.” China, meanwhile, has been steps ahead for years and “has the world’s leading hypersonic missile arsenal,” according to the U.S. Department of Defense’s 2025 report to Congress.

It has been revealed that kreitz pointed to several reasons for the gap, starting with how the U.S. defense industry develops and builds weapons. He noted the Pentagon has often prioritized the most advanced technology without giving enough thought to cost or how easily it can be manufactured. Cost-plus contracts, which reimburse contractors for their expenses, also give companies less incentive to control costs.

The aerospace and defense industry also suffers from failing to test hardware early and often, Kreitz said, arguing that fewer tests mean slower learning and development.

“Unfortunately, our adversaries very much took the opposite approach,” Kreitz said on stage. “The Chinese have tested and iterated very, very fast, and they’ve been relentlessly focused on industrializing and manufacturing these weapons at a very large scale.”.

Kreitz and fellow cofounders Sean Pitt and Bryon Hargis left SpaceX in 2022 to start Castelion, aiming to disrupt the defense industry by building weapons faster, cheaper, and at a much larger scale.

In just four years, Castelion has grown to more than 400 employees, reached a $13 billion valuation, and secured multiple Pentagon contracts. In September, the U.S. Navy awarded the tech giant a contract worth up to $200 million for Blackbeard, its low-cost hypersonic missile.

Much of that success, Kreitz stated, comes from the engineering culture they learned at SpaceX—and can be traced back even further to NASA’s Apollo program.

“It hearkens back to the golden age of American aerospace in the 50s and 60s: get to hardware as promptly as possible, test as early as possible, iterate as fast as possible,” he mentioned.

Castelion is also willing to bring more manufacturing in-house rather than rely on outside suppliers when supply chain complications get in the way.

“Everything has to be backwards planned, from how do we scale production of this weapon—the iteration cycles and the testing, especially though, that just unlocks learning at a really, really rapid pace,” Kreitz added.

Castelion is riding a wave of investment in defense technology. In the third quarter of 2026, defense startups raised a record $2.5 billion—contributing to a total defense tech VC value of $67.4 billion across 726 deals this year, according to PitchBook.

Leading the pack in terms of valuation is Anduril, which raised funding in May at a $61 billion valuation and has since explored a potential deal that would nearly double that figure.

But Kreitz thinks the boom has created a bubble—and not every company will survive the coming shakeout.

“There is froth in the market,” Kreitz remarked. “I think that there will be a shakeout at some point. That’s the truth.”.

Some companies have promising technology and products but lack the ability to bring them to market or manufacture them at scale, Kreitz noted. Others may ultimately be acquired as the industry consolidates. For Castelion, the strategy is to focus more on actually building its business.

“Our approach to weathering this is focus on execution, focus on operations, focus on manufacturing, get ourselves to scale and free cash flow generation as soon as possible to sort of immunize us to any of the noise that might be occurring in the capital markets,” Kreitz said.

FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange.
  • Recent findings suggest that MEXC says user assets remain secure.
  • Sources indicate that on November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

Recent findings suggest that MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

Sources indicate that on November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

In a recent development, on the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

Industry observers note that the ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

Recent findings suggest that MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange notes it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, looks to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

According to recent reports, two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN indicates the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

In a recent development, the charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN says MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN notes the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

Sources indicate that the order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary consumers anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN claims plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Recent findings suggest that before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

FinCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

According to recent reports, according to a recent Reuters report citing an internal document, Amazon is working on a secret initiative called World Product Graph to catalog products across the Internet, including items that it doesn’t at the moment sell. In a recent development, world Product Graph could ensure that Amazon is the first place shoppers visit to figure out what they want to purchase. That would give Amazon a stronger hold over the product research space, challenging Google while giving shoppers another reason to choose it over Walmart and other retailers.

The project could also help Amazon navigate a shift in how people shop. Currently, some shoppers are using AI agents to research products and potentially make purchases. AI agents need reliable product information to make recommendations, which is something the World Product Graph could provide.

If the proposal becomes reality, it could offer Amazon an advantage that goes beyond competitive pricing. The site could offer information that makes other shopping sites feel less useful by comparison.

In a statement to Reuters, Amazon stated it is “constantly working on newly introduced ideas and technologies.”.

“Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current looks,” the company mentioned in the statement.

The leaked document presents the proposal as a future press announcement, with October 1, 2027, as a target launch date. Reuters was not able to confirm a timeline or if Amazon would move forward with the looks.

Amazon currently has a stronger hold on shoppers who know what they want rather than those who are still deciding. A 2025 Morgan Stanley research report cited by Reuters found that 57% of online shoppers began product research on Google, compared with just 16% on Amazon.

Once shoppers have a specific product in mind, the rankings reverse. Amazon becomes the leading starting point, accounting for 41% of searches, compared with 23% for Google and 18% for Walmart.

Google right now leads in discovery, while Amazon has the advantage when customers arrive with a clearer purchase in mind.

#6010. Tech Report: He Became a Chick-fil-A Franchise Operator at Age 26. Now He Runs Two of Its Highest-Grossing Restaurants.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1335 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: He Became a Chick-fil-A Franchise Operator at Age 26. Now He Runs Two of Its Highest-Grossing Restaurants.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hurst had just graduated from college.
  • “This is what I did,” Hurst indicates in a upcoming interview with Entrepreneur.
  • In a recent development, the opportunity offered him a chance to learn the business directly from an operator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2010, Brandon J. Hurst had just graduated from college. He had three options on the table. First, he could stay at Alabama State University, where he had received his Bachelor’s degree, to get a Master’s degree in accounting. Second, he could apply to law school and then go work on Wall Street. Or third, he could take a $12-an-hour job in Chicago working at Chick-fil-A with no guaranteed career path in sight.

“This is what I did,” Hurst indicates in a upcoming interview with Entrepreneur. “Two weeks after graduation, I packed everything I owned and drove 14 hours straight to start a brand new life in Chicago to work inside of a Chick-fil-A restaurant.”.

In a recent development, the opportunity offered him a chance to learn the business directly from an operator. He moved there to become a director of operations at the branch — an opportunity he couldn’t pass up.

“I knew whatever I would be doing, I had to be in some type of entrepreneurial capacity,” he says.

Chick-fil-A offers an unusually affordable way to enter the restaurant business: Its initial franchise fee is $10,000 and has stayed that way for the past 50 years, per The New York Post. Applicants must use their own money, not borrowed or gifted funds, to pay the franchise fee.

However, that payment does not buy ownership of a restaurant.

Instead, Chick-fil-A selects operators to run locations that the company finances. The company handles major startup expenses, including construction and equipment, and retains ownership of the restaurant’s assets. Operators manage the business rather than acquire an asset they can eventually sell.

It has been revealed that that differs from traditional franchising, where franchisees typically fund the startup investment and own a business operating under another firm’s brand. ADP puts most franchise startup costs between $100,000 and $300,000, with restaurants and hotels among the most expensive options.

According to recent reports, chick-fil-A’s franchise business is also highly competitive. The Post reported that about 100,000 people apply annually to be operators, and of those, 200 are selected, or about 0.2%.

Selected operators must work full-time in the business and divest other non-passive business interests. Chick-fil-A explicitly says the program is not a passive investment. Operators do not receive a traditional corporate salary. Instead, their income comes from a profit-sharing model.

They earn a percentage of the store’s net profits and typically take home anywhere from $200,000 to $400,000 a year. High-performing operators earn more than $500,000 annually.

According to recent reports, so operators need comparatively little upfront capital, but they do not build equity in the restaurant. They cannot sell it or pass it down to their children when they retire.

It has been revealed that in 2012, Hurst was selected for Chick-fil-A’s leadership development program. For the next three years, he helped operators launch restaurants around the country.

According to recent reports, the work gave him repeated opportunities to practice opening a business without immediately taking responsibility for his own. He supported 14 operators, 12 of whom were external candidates who had never owned or worked at a Chick-fil-A restaurant.

Industry observers note that “You ever heard the saying, ‘If you want to master something, teach it’?” Hurst claims. “That’s exactly what I had the opportunity to do.”.

The experience let him repeatedly practice opening restaurants before taking responsibility for one himself.

In April 2015, at age 26, Hurst opened his first Chick-fil-A restaurant in downtown Baltimore. He wanted to help Chick-fil-A figure out how to operate in dense urban neighborhoods, where restaurants couldn’t rely on the large drive-thrus familiar to suburban customers.

Hurst was in Baltimore for five years before passing the torch to other local operators and relocating to Brooklyn, Fresh York. He opened his first Brooklyn restaurant across from Barclays Center in 2019, followed by a second in Clinton Hill in November 2024.

Industry observers note that today, he describes his restaurants as among Chick-fil-A’s highest-grossing locations. According to Restaurant Business, Chick-fil-A’s stand-alone restaurants averaged nearly $9.2 million in sales in 2025. Its busiest location brings in more than $20 million annually, while its top-performing mall restaurant recorded $14.4 million in sales in 2025.

Presented with these statistics, Hurst stated his restaurants were “well north of those numbers,” without providing an exact figure.

He credits the neighborhoods, customers attending Barclays Center events and, above all, his employees, for his success.

Chick-fil-A stood out to Hurst because he wouldn’t have to create a concept or a brand-newly introduced menu.

“Although I have a strong entrepreneurial spirit, I don’t have a whole lot of patience for building something from the ground up,” he claims. “I can cook, but I’m more of an operational strategy and leadership development person.”.

Chick-fil-A already provided a brand and systems that allowed Hurst to “hit the ground running” and focus on his strengths.

Recent findings suggest that the financial barrier to entry was also notable. Hurst was able to open his first Chick-fil-A restaurant at age 26 because of the relatively low $10,000 upfront cost when compared to other franchises.

According to recent reports, hurst indicates future franchise operators should determine their capacity to shoulder risk, then ask what they are willing to sacrifice. “You may have the financial means, but are you ready to invest the time and resources it will take?” he asks.

Hurst notes his growth depends on retaining employees.

Recent findings suggest that to that end, he purchased a multi-family building in Brooklyn where team members can live at below-market rents. He also provides access to free mental health care, including up to 10 sessions with a therapist, and telehealth services for employees and their households. Eligible college students can receive reimbursement for textbooks.

The numbers show that his investments are working. He indicates his leaders have an average tenure of about four years. For regular team members, retention rates greater than 12 to 16 months are a win.

Hurst claims that hiring is about finding people who want to serve others. One question he asks is: “Tell me about a time you wanted to give up and why you didn’t.”.

The answer helps him understand how someone handles adversity in a busy, high-pressure restaurant. Another question he asks is: “How do you define care for yourself?” The answer helps him understand what meaningful support might look like for that person.

But supporting employees also means allowing them to take responsibility. Hurst notes one of his ongoing challenges is building an organization that doesn’t depend too heavily on him.

“If every major decision, relationship or problem” has to come through the founder, he notes, “then I really haven’t built the capacity to scale.”.

Hurst hired an executive assistant about five years ago, who helped him organize his calendar and create space for other work, including his forthcoming book, Outthink Yourself, which comes out in January.

Sources indicate that “I wrote the book for anyone who is navigating growth, whether you’re in your first job leading a team or building a business,” Hurst states. “This book was a four-year process in the making.”.

Hurst organizes his approach to growth around three stages: See, become and build.

The first is understanding the opportunity, problem or risk in front of you. The second is identifying the skills and capabilities you need to pursue it. The third is building systems that make progress sustainable.

In a recent development, he traces that framework through his own career. Assessing the Chicago job required him to get comfortable with uncertainty. Training other operators helped him become a stronger leader. Running two restaurants required him to build teams that could sustain the business.

In a recent development, his next ambitions include expanding his Chick-fil-A portfolio and working with entrepreneurs through speaking engagements and training workshops. He has also begun developing a second book focused more directly on putting his ideas into practice.

It has been revealed that “More locations, more books,” Hurst states. “I do have very high aspirations for myself.”.

According to prominent analyst EGRAG Crypto, the weakness is no coincidence, pointing to three key factors that could explain XRP’s sharper decline and signal why the token may continue struggling as bearish sentiment grips the market.

Crypto analyst EGRAG Crypto has highlighted XRP’s worsening performance against Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and Solana (SOL) amid November’s broader cryptocurrency market drawdown. In a Nov. 10 post on X, the pundit noted the striking difference in losses since November 4, showing that Ripple’s XRP has suffered the steepest decline among the four major cryptocurrencies.

According to EGRAG Crypto’s figures, XRP has plunged 23.4% since November 4, significantly more than ETH’s 18.2% decline and SOL’s 17% drop. BTC has demonstrated greater resilience, losing just 10.4% over the same period.

Sources indicate that the figures raise an vital question: Why is XRP bleeding considerably more than its major competitors? EGRAG Crypto has pointed to three possible factors behind the token’s disproportionate weakness, offering a closer look at the selling pressure weighing on the Ripple-linked token.

It has been revealed that the first factor is leveraged long liquidations, which EGRAG assigns a 30% probability. According to the analyst, forced liquidations of bullish positions, combined with weak buying demand, could be accelerating XRP’s fall. When leveraged traders are forced to close their positions during a downturn, the resulting selling pressure can trigger further losses and deepen an existing market correction.

Sources indicate that the second possibility, which carries a 20% probability, is selling by early XRP holders. EGRAG suggests that longtime investors, often referred to as OGs, could be taking profits and rotating their capital into other cryptocurrencies. Such activity could increase selling pressure on XRP, particularly if large holders decide to reduce their exposure amid uncertain market conditions.

Recent findings suggest that finally, EGRAG assigns the highest probability, 50%, to what the expert describes as market manipulation or a deliberate liquidity hunt. Under this scenario, sharp price movements could be designed to trigger stop-loss orders and force weaker traders out of their positions before a potential recovery. The analyst believes this could explain why XRP is experiencing disproportionately heavy selling compared with other major cryptocurrencies.

Notably, these percentages represent EGRAG Crypto’s personal probability-based assessment rather than independently verified evidence of the causes behind XRP’s decline.

Beyond identifying the possible reasons behind XRP’s sharper decline, EGRAG Crypto has also highlighted several vital price levels that could determine the token’s next move. The analyst identified the $1.00-$1.04 range as a critical stabilization zone, suggesting that holding this area could help XRP establish a floor amid the ongoing selling pressure.

On the upside, EGRAG believes bulls must first reclaim the $1.15 level before targeting $1.25. A recovery above these thresholds could signal improving buying momentum and offer some relief to investors after the recent losses.

Sources indicate that sharing a personal assessment, EGRAG Crypto said the ongoing price action appears more consistent with market manipulation designed to frighten newer investors into selling. However, the analyst raised a bigger question about whale activity, questioning whether deep-pocketed XRP holders are using the downturn to accumulate more tokens or adding to the selling pressure by offloading their holdings.

Sources indicate that ultimately, how whales respond to the current market weakness could offer important clues about XRP’s next direction. If large holders are absorbing the available supply, the sell-off could eventually lose momentum. Conversely, continued whale selling could make an already difficult recovery even harder for the sixth-largest cryptocurrency.

Major crypto exchange Coinbase is set to suspend trading in 12 crypto trading pairs as part of an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity on the platform. This decision affects two trading pairs involving Cardano (ADA) and Stellar (XLM): ADA/ETH and XLM/BTC.

In a recent development, coinbase said it regularly monitors the markets on its exchange and, in line with this, trading will be suspended on the named markets on November 25, 2026. In an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity, Coinbase will be removing a number of non-USD trading pairs for supported assets.

According to an announcement, Coinbase will suspend trading on the following markets on November 25, 2026, at or around 12 PM ET: APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP, SNX-GBP.

However, Coinbase Advanced Trade users in eligible regions can still trade these assets in the USD order books.

In light of this, APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP have been moved to limit-only mode on Coinbase Exchange and Coinbase Advanced.

In recent delistings, Coinbase has disabled trading for Balancer (BAL) and Tensor (TNSR), but people will continue to have the ability to withdraw their funds at any time.

According to recent reports, the suspension of trading for Stargate Finance (STG) and Vulcan Forged (PYR) has also been postponed to November 20, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Based on recent reviews, Coinbase will suspend trading for Ampleforth Governance Token (FORTH) on November 23, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Trading for Neon EVM (NEON) and Syndicate (SYND) will be suspended on November 16, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET.

Spot trading for Pearl (PEARL) will go live on November 13, 2026. The opening of the PEARL-USD trading pair will begin at or after 9 AM PT, if liquidity conditions are met, in regions where trading is supported.

Perpetual futures trading for GRAM, GRASS, QNT and ZRO will go live on November 13, 2026, at or after 12:00 PM UTC.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm.

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a organization’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a organization’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company noted.

Recent findings suggest that it works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the tech giant said.

It has been revealed that the pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

In a recent development, “Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”.

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Industry observers note that guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

Industry observers note that the Crunchbase Unicorn Board is a curated list that includes private unicorn companies with post-money valuations of $1 billion or more and is based on Crunchbase data. Fresh companies are added to the Unicorn Board as they reach the $1 billion valuation mark as part of a funding round.

The unicorn board does not reflect internal company valuations — such as those set via a 409a process for employee stock options — as these differ from, and are more likely to be lower than, a priced funding round. We also do not adjust valuations based on investor writedowns, which change quarterly, as different investors will not value the same company consistently within the same quarter.

Funding to unicorn companies includes all private financings to companies that are tagged as unicorns, as well as those that have since graduated to The Exited Unicorn Board.

Exits analyzed here only include the first time a company exits.

Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was declared, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price.

#6001. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1352 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text.
  • Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft.
  • The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

It has been revealed that the SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

According to recent reports, the abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets notes it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

In a recent development, that delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Recent findings suggest that nothing in the record indicates what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Industry observers note that existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ states a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency prepares for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

According to recent reports, commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move swiftly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Recent findings suggest that rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

In a recent development, crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

Industry observers note that the sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

According to recent reports, the package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

“This is a great place to buy BTC,” Lunde stated.

Among the indicators Lunde considers is the fact that BTC has returned to its 200-week moving average (MA). This is a long-term technical indicator widely tracked by crypto traders. It’s used to identify potential market bottoms.

According to Lunde, the daily Relative Strength Index (RSI) for Bitcoin has fallen to 25, which demonstrates that the market has become oversold.

In a recent development, whenever the RSI goes below 30, it suggests that the asset has been oversold, experiencing heavy selling pressure. It doesn’t necessarily mean that the price will reverse higher.

Lunde also noted that Bitcoin has experienced the fifth-largest wave of exchange-traded fund (ETF) outflows on record. There’s also been a large reduction in leverage on Bitcoin ETFs.

Exposure to 2x leveraged ETFs has now reached a level not seen in the last 2.5 years. That’s a massive reduction in leverage on the asset. “So, speculative stuff is off,” Lunde stated.

“Don’t press the red panic button!” Lunde added.

Lunde's bullish take comes as Bitcoin suffered yet another devastating sell-off on Friday, Nov. 13. The price of Bitcoin dropped below the psychologically significant $70,000 level for the first time since August.

BTC dropped as low as $67,770, marking its lowest price in the last 12 weeks. The cryptocurrency’s prolonged decline continues.

Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.

On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling latest details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco company.

Industry observers note that anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That mentioned, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX’s June debut.

The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment looks.

For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic prepares to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year.

For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this.

The organization claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

The total offering is for 825 million shares, of which 23.6 million will be from selling shareholders.↩.

Rakuten also holds funds tracking Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana, and these positions were worth roughly $6.42 million combined at the end of the quarter on Sept. 30, 2026.

Besides, Rakuten owns $263,632 of the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF and $150,728 of the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF.

U.S. rules require any institutional manager holding more than $100 million in U.S. exchange-listed securities to disclose its portfolio every quarter, no matter where it's based. Rakuten Group holds about $1.4 billion in U.S. equities, and most of that amount is in shares of satellite operator AST SpaceMobile. The Rakuten ecosystem spans more than 70 services, from the Rakuten Ichiba marketplace and carrier Rakuten Mobile to banks and brokerages. According to Rakuten, these services have more than 100 million owners in Japan and more than 2.1 billion users worldwide.

The latest filing comes amid outflows from spot XRP ETFs. According to SoSoValue, the funds lost $10.42 million on Nov. 9 and another $7.62 million on Nov. 10, and there were no flows on Nov. 11 and Nov. 12. On Oct. 28, the total net assets of the funds stood at $1.51 billion.

Still, the cumulative net inflow of spot XRP ETFs stands at $1.79 billion, and the total net assets of the funds are $1.16 billion, or 1.77% of the market cap of XRP. Finally, the Bitwise XRP ETF is the largest of the five spot XRP funds, and its net assets stand at $420.29 million, according to SoSoValue.

Exclusive: Nubank Alum Raises $14M For Colombia’s Palomma To Tackle Rent Payments, Landlord Financing

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2020, Cipriano Echavarría was working at Morgan Stanley in Newly introduced York and weighing his next career move when he noticed a plaque on his desk.
  • Vélez was not only a fellow Colombian from his hometown of Medellín, but also the founder of Brazilian digital bank Nubank.
  • According to recent reports, it turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 2020, Cipriano Echavarría was working at Morgan Stanley in Newly introduced York and weighing his next career move when he noticed a plaque on his desk. Among the names of people who had sat there before him was David Vélez.

He looked up the name. Vélez was not only a fellow Colombian from his hometown of Medellín, but also the founder of Brazilian digital bank Nubank. Echavarría took a photo of the plaque and messaged him on LinkedIn, asking for career advice.

According to recent reports, it turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team. By late 2020, Echavarría had returned home to join it, with prepares to eventually start a firm of his own.

Now Echavarría’s Medellín-based startup, Palomma, has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Mexican venture firm Cometa to expand its financial services business for landlords, tenants and property managers, Crunchbase News has exclusively learned.

According to recent reports, the financing brings Palomma’s total funding to $14 million, including $4 million in previously undisclosed funding, according to Echavarría, its co-founder and CEO. Participants include Volpe Capital, Clocktower Technology Ventures, Tekton Ventures, Simma Capital and Yango Ventures, alongside existing investors Y Combinator, 17Sigma, Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures.

According to recent reports, palomma says its annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million. It processes about $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia. It estimates $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume.

The organization will use the funding to expand in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare to enter other markets. It is considering Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market, although Echavarría noted Colombia remains the priority.

“We want to win Colombia,” he stated in an interview.

Industry observers note that palomma’s business combines software that helps property managers handle leasing inquiries, customer service and collections with a payments system for collecting rent and paying landlords. Those relationships let it sell financing, rental guarantees, and other financial products to tenants and property owners.

After nearly two years at Nubank, Echavarría went on to found Palomma with Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo, MIT-trained engineers with experience at Meta, Cobre and JP Morgan. The founders entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was largely flat during the first year, Echavarría said. But then property managers began asking for help collecting rent.

It soon became apparent that there were problems on both sides of the transaction. Tenants paid rent early in the month, but got their paychecks in twice-monthly installments. Meanwhile, landlords depended on rental income but struggled to borrow against it or protect themselves when tenants stopped paying. Property managers handled collections and payouts through labor-intensive processes, Echavarría said.

Rather than acquire tenants and landlords as customers individually, Palomma decided to reach them through the companies managing their properties.

The team decided, “let’s basically use the property managers as a distribution channel,” Echavarría recalled.

Property managers get access to Palomma’s AI software, which handles tasks such as leasing conversations. It then offers to process their rent payments. Those payments give the firm a record of rental income and tenant payment histories that it can use to assess applicants for financial products.

According to recent reports, from there, Palomma offers services for both tenants and landlords. Palomma Plus gives tenants rewards and credit-building benefits, while Palomma Advance lets landlords collect up to 12 months of future rental income upfront. Palomma Protect covers rental income if a tenant defaults. The manufacturer is also developing Palomma Flex, which would let tenants split their monthly rent into two installments.

Property managers pay a subscription fee for the AI software, and Palomma earns a percentage of rent through its payments and financial services.

Getting customers to adopt more of its services has helped drive Palomma’s growth. The firm reports net revenue retention of 390% after 12 months, meaning revenue from an existing group of customers nearly quadrupled, even after accounting for customers who left or spent less.

Sources indicate that overall, the decision to combine AI leasing software, payments and financial services reflects Echavarría’s view of what it takes to build a large business in Latin America. He pointed to U.S. companies such as EliseAI, Bilt, TheGuarantors and Flex as comparisons for different parts of Palomma’s business. Echavarría believes that reaching a similar scale in Latin America requires a wider range of products.

According to recent reports, “In the U.S., you can build one solution and be really large because the market allows it,” he said. “In Latin America, if you want to be really large, you need to do all the things.”.

AI also helps decide which tenants qualify for rental guarantees. Palomma’s leasing agent communicates through WhatsApp and collects application documents. The company claims that it can then deliver an approval in under 30 seconds. The company draws on information from leasing conversations and rental payment behavior to assess applicants.

The company’s rental guarantees put Palomma on the hook if tenants don’t pay. The startup initially takes on that risk itself, but Echavarría told Crunchbase News it was working to finalize a partnership with an insurer that would share the risk and let Palomma offer more guarantees.

Industry observers note that the startup is also using AI to keep its team small. As of Nov. 4, it had 18 employees, up from about 14 when it closed its Series A roughly three weeks earlier. A single customer service employee works alongside AI agents to support the roughly 200,000 tenants paying rent through Palomma’s platform, Echavarría mentioned.

The startup operates on the premise that AI can make real estate financial services cheaper to provide, much as mobile technology helped digital banks compete with lenders that maintained large branch networks. Longer term, Palomma also intends to expand beyond rentals into homeowners association payments and residential property transactions.

Pepe Bolaños, managing partner at Cometa, mentioned Palomma stood out for its founding team and the opportunity to modernize Latin America’s fragmented rental market. In Colombia alone, nearly 8 million households rent their homes, he noted.

“We look for companies tackling markets where outdated processes create an opportunity to build a proprietary data asset that can be leveraged and monetized through AI,” he wrote via email.

Industry observers note that bolaños pointed to Echavarría’s experience helping scale Nubank, and Monsalve and del Campo’s technical and financial backgrounds. In roughly 18 months, Palomma grew to process around $130 million in monthly rental payments and serve more than 200,000 tenants with about 14 employees, he said.

Sources indicate that “That kind of execution is unusual. It convinced us that this team has what it takes to build a much larger business,” he added.

Industry observers note that unlike competitors focused on individual services, Palomma combines rent collection, tenant screening and rental guarantees, gathering data throughout the process, Bolaños remarked. Directly processing payments gives it insight into tenant behavior that can improve underwriting, flag potential defaults and support newly introduced financial products, while AI helps automate operations.

“We believe the combination of distribution, proprietary payment data and AI gives Palomma a competitive advantage that can become stronger as the manufacturer grows,” he noted.

Industry observers note that stellar (XLM), the blockchain co-founded by Jed McCaleb, has become the leader in daily market cap growth for tokenized real-world asset (RWA) funds, according to Token Terminal data published by the RWA Foundation. Over the 24 hours to Nov. 13, the market cap of tokenized funds on Stellar went up by $44.9 million, and the network surpassed both Ethereum and Solana.

Over the same period, the market cap of tokenized funds on Solana, Ethereum and zkSync Era increased by $29 million, $10.8 million and $3.5 million, respectively.

It has been revealed that stellar is currently the second-largest blockchain for tokenized funds after Ethereum, according to Token Terminal. Over the past year, the RWA market on Stellar has grown roughly sixfold and reached $4.67 billion, according to rwa.xyz. At press time, the price of XLM stands at $0.1476.

According to the Stellar Development Foundation, Stellar was designed with the requirements of banks and transfer agents in mind. In this context, the compliance tools are built into the base layer of the network, and an issuer can vet investors through trustlines, freeze accounts and claw back assets.

Transactions on Stellar settle in 3 to 5 seconds, and the fees on the network are measured in fractions of a cent. Besides, customers can move funds to and from fiat currencies through local providers, which are called anchors on Stellar.

In a recent development, franklin Templeton's BENJI money market fund has run on Stellar since 2021, and it was the first U.S. mutual fund on a public blockchain.

Recent findings suggest that today, Spiko, Ondo and WisdomTree are also building their own funds and tokenized U.S. Treasuries on Stellar. Spiko offers euro funds managed by Amundi, and Ondo has debuted its USDY token on the network.

In May 2026, DTCC and the Stellar Development Foundation revealed that the Depository Trust Company (DTC) will tokenize the assets it holds in custody on Stellar. According to DTCC, DTC-tokenized assets are expected to become available on the network in the first half of 2027.

On Nov. 12, DTCC also announced that it will connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.
  • Recent findings suggest that zipline and Walmart reached a upcoming multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States.
  • On the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Manufacturer, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.

Recent findings suggest that zipline and Walmart reached a upcoming multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. The two companies have had a drone delivery agreement since 2021, but this deal is a significant jump from the 21 active drone delivery sites they have together today.

On the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Manufacturer, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest, and Salesforce Ventures. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.

The company, which has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software, noted it plans to use the funds to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire more workers to build out a nationwide drone delivery network.

Founded in 2014, Zipline got its start in Africa, where it used its autonomous drones to deliver blood in Rwanda, and later expanded to Ghana and Nigeria. The California-based organization began its first operations in the U.S. in 2020, ferrying medical equipment and supplies to Novant Health in North Carolina. The following year, it struck a deal with Walmart.

But it was in 2022 that Zipline’s business really started to take off in the United States. Zipline received its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration that year, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the firm to complete long-range commercial drone deliveries. It has locked in a number of partnerships since then, including with Uber earlier this year.

Zipline now uses its drones to deliver food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several cities in the United States, and Japan. Zipline’s home delivery service uses Zipline’s Platform 2 drones, which are designed to carry up to eight pounds and travel to customers within a 10-mile radius. Its larger Platform 1 drones are used for long-range deliveries for enterprise, business, and government that can cover 120 miles round trip.

Industry observers note that the company said Thursday that its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October of this year. This latest funding aims to push that metric even higher.

#5992. Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1057 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like AI is cracking a fresh math problem every week.
  • Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground.
  • On Wednesday, the company confirmed it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like AI is cracking a fresh math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscriptsclaiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. But even the computer checks meant to confirm those results can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.

Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.

On Wednesday, the company confirmed it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.

Recent findings suggest that woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.

The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.

Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.

Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.

Recent findings suggest that for a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.

That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.

“Things that are significant and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”.

The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.

“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong stated.

To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” said Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.”.

Sources indicate that axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own.

It has been revealed that the result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan mentioned.

It has been revealed that until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan said. “Well, now they do.”.

It has been revealed that axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply: “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.”.

Mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code.

Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does.

It has been revealed that “We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan noted. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build upcoming infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.”.

The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop.

“You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong mentioned. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.”.

Industry observers note that hong is confident enough in that approach to problem a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”.

Tech Report: VCs Are Still Chasing Protein, Even As Fake Meat Falls Out Of Favor
